2000:
Welcome to the Imperialism II: Age of Exploration Tutorial. When you click ‘Start the first Episode’, below, you will begin Episode 1 of a series of 19 episodes. Each episode sets a goal for you which you must complete to end the episode.

During the tutorial a small feedback window remains open on your screen. You can move this window to any location you like (for instance to see what is underneath it) but it will be present on screen during all 19 episodes. The top part of the window shows feedback about the action you just took. The lower part prompts a possible next action.

You may review the background and goals for the episode by clicking the arrow button on the feedback window. You may consult on-line help briefings by clicking on the question mark button found on all main game screens. 

When you have completed all 19 episodes you will be familiar with the basics of Imperialism II. You will be ready to assume your rightful place as a Monarch of a colonial Great Power.
2001:
Congratulations, the Builder has completed developing a Grain Farm, and you have completed Episode 1.  

As your Empire expands in future episodes, you will want to continue using your Builder to increase the amount of Grain, Meat, and other resources available to your capital city. Developing natural resources will be an important activity throughout the game since you need resources to feed your laborers and military units, to construct materials that permit further expansion, and to make profits through trade.
2002:
Congratulations, your Engineer has completed building road that connects a Grain Farm to the capital city, and you have completed Episode 2. This Grain will be automatically transported to the city where it will be eaten by industrial workers.

You can verify that the Grain farm tile is connected in two ways: hold the cursor over the tile and look at the help text that appears in the top right of the screen. It will show that "Max Transport" has gone from 0 to 1. You could also info-click on the tile to get a detailed report about the tile. Note that you did not have to build road all the way into the Grain Farm tile --just being adjacent to road is sufficient.

As your Empire expands in future episodes, you will want to continue using your Engineer to connect the developments made by the Builder.
2003:
Congratulations,  your Explorer just discovered a hidden mineral deposit, and you have completed Episode 3.  

Continue to use your Explorer each turn to look for valuable resources in your homeland. Don’t forget that prospected minerals are not usable until the Builder develops them.
2004:
Congratulations,  your Builder and Engineer have completed the goal of connecting two more developments to the capital, and you have completed Episode 4. You now have the start of a good road network.

The developments which you have made so far  are all level 1 developments, which means simply that they produce one unit of resources (such as timber, or grain) every turn. Later technologies will permit the Builder to work on the same terrain tiles again increasing the resource output of the development on the tile. Technologies will also lead to improved roads capable of transporting these additional resources to the capital city.
2005:
Congratulations,  you have produced Lumber, Cast Iron and Fabric, thus completing Episode 5.

The Builder uses Lumber and Cast Iron each time he develops a tile. The Engineer uses Lumber and Cast Iron each time he builds road. You will use Fabric in the next Episode, to recruit new laborers into the city.
2006:
Congratulations,  you have your industrial workers set to make Fabric, Lumber and Cast Iron every turn, as long as the resources are available. You have completed Episode 6. 

In the next episode, you will learn how to transport resources which are too far from your capital to be quickly reached via road.
2007:
The Engineer has completed building the port, which completes Episode 7. 

Now that you have two ports (your capital and the one just constructed) your Engineer may build roads connected to either one. 

However, keep in mind that the resources gathered from roads connected only to the new (non-capital) port must be moved by ship from the port back to the capital city. As you will learn in the next episode there are advantages to land transport. 

It will be a good idea later in the game to connect all your ports (on the same continent) with roads to the capital.  For now, ports are an efficient way to gain distant resources.
2008:
Congratulations,  you have succeeded in transporting at least four units of resources by ship. You have completed Episode 8.  

In future episodes, as your Empire expands into other continents, you may develop several separate land transport networks joined only by ports. This type of expansion requires the construction of a much larger fleet since these resources must be moved by ship to the capital. Ships are also used for other purposes including trade, controlling the seas, and exploration.
2009:
Congratulations,  your ship has uncovered the coastline of the New World. You have completed Episode 9. 

Generally, it is a good idea to keep one ship exploring until the entire coast is mapped. Some find it convenient to order their ships while using the zoomed out map.

Send your Explorer to search the interior of these new lands. He exposes all the tiles around him. The New World contains exotic resources not found in the Old World, such as Cotton, Tobacco, Silver and Diamonds.  Some of these products (sugar cane, tobacco, and furs) are required to produce luxuries demanded by more highly trained workers.
2010:
Congratulations, your ship or Explorer has uncovered a tribal capital, completing Episode 10. This makes it possible to conduct diplomacy and trade with this tribe for the first time.  Continue exploring to find the other tribal capitals.

The next episodes introduce diplomacy and trade.  The episodes use the Old World for the demonstration. Keep in mind, however, that these same strategies for trade and diplomacy apply to those tribes whose capitals you have located.
2011:
Congratulations, by building a Consulate and granting a trade subsidy,  you have become the favored trade partner of a Minor Nation and completed Episode 11.

The inter-dependency of trade and diplomatic success will be a recurring theme during your rule. The long term purpose of diplomacy is getting other countries to choose to join your Empire. But the short term goal is to gain a steady trade supply of the resources that the other nation produces. 

Once you have become the favorite trading partner of a minor nation, you can count on trade offers each turn. This is especially useful at the beginning of the game when your own nation has not yet developed its transport network.
2012:
Congratulations, you have successfully sold a material and bought a resource. You have completed Episode 12.  

As the game continues, you should complete as many trades as possible with minor nations with whom you have Trade Consulates. Each of those trade deals improves relations between your Great Power and the Minor Nation. 

You now know the two methods--transport and trade-- of gaining resources (or materials) for production. Generally you should purchase resources that are in short supply in your own country. Buying materials on the market is often a bad idea because of the high costs. It is wiser to rely on your own production to turn resources into materials.
2013:
Your new military unit is stationed at your capital city. You have completed Episode 13.  

Your new military unit will come up in the unit cycle after the civilians. The best thing to do with it at this point is give it orders to defend the capital (click the right-most unit order button on the toolbar).

This first unit is merely the beginning of your military buildup. (Even pacifist nations must have strong defense forces.) The next episode covers the uses of naval and military forces to expand your Empire .
2014:
Congratulations, you completed Episode 14.   Your force of 3 new Pikemen is garrisoned at the capital. 

This force should be able to conquer a province in the New World.  In the next episode, you will use your navy to establish a beachhead in the New World, so that you can send in the troops.
2015:
Congratulations, you have established a landing zone, or beachhead, in the New World and completed Episode 15. In the next episode you will send troops into the province with the beachhead.

The fleet maintaining the beachhead is safe enough for now, because the tribes have no naval forces to threaten it. However, if you were fighting another Great Power, your ships could be intercepted. In that case it would be necessary to send enough force to protect your fleet from hostile ships.
2016:
Congratulations, your attack on the New World province was successful. You have completed Episode 16. That province is now part of your Empire. It appears as your color on the diplomacy map. 

Your civilian units can now develop this new territory in the same way they have been developing your home country.  An important first step is the construction of a port. Roads built out from this port gather the commodities of your new province. 

Some commodities, such as sugar and tobacco, are only available in the New World and are essential for the long term development of your Great Power. You should keep a garrison in the New World to protect your conquests.
2017:
Congratulations, you are the proud owner of land in the New World and you have completed Episode 17.  Other Great Powers would have to declare war on you before attacking that province, so you are protecting the Tribes while you exploit their resources. 

The next episode will cover the financial benefits of owning land in Minor Nations.
2018:
You have realized Overseas Profits from the developed land tile you purchased and completed Episode 18.  Keep exploring. Remember that in the New World mountains could hide gems or gold, hills could contain silver and deserts could yield diamonds. Even spices make a valuable contribution to your economy. 

Buy more land. Send in your Builder and Engineer to develop new resources and connect them to a port or to the Tribal capital so they can get sold and you can make more money.
2019:
Congratulations, your research efforts and patience have been rewarded: you have completed the discovery of a new technology and Episode 19.

Each new technology expands the capabilities of your Empire, provided that your economy is developed sufficiently to take advantage of the new opportunities. In a game of Imperialism II, you must balance your technological growth with the growth of the infrastructure required to benefit from a new technology.
2020: It is the year 1670. Now that have completed the tutorial and learned the rudiments of running an Empire, the time has come for you to assume your rightful place as full monarch.
2101:
Your country is still rural and undeveloped. While the people may be surviving by living off the land, they are not producing anything that could be used by large scale industry, nor are they producing enough food to feed the industrial work force in your capital.

To get terrain tiles to produce useful quantities, you must develop them with the Builder.  When a Builder develops a tile, a small structure appears. You will see that the tiles adjacent to your capital city are already developed. 

When you close this window, a smaller window will appear. At the top it provides feedback on your last action. The lower text helps prompt your next action.
2102:
Welcome to Episode 2. You are getting a new unit, the Engineer, and access to the unit cycling buttons on the toolbar.

Developed resources are of no use unless they are transported to the capital city. The main function for the Engineer is to build a road network connecting developed resources to the capital city, where they can be used for industry or trade.

Resource tiles are considered "connected" if they have a road going through them, or are adjacent to a tile that has road in it. Resource tiles adjacent to the capital city or to other ports are also connected.

Click the question mark button on the lower right of the Main Map screen for explanations of road networks and of how to use the unit cycle buttons shown in the toolbar.
2103:
Welcome to Episode 3. You are getting a new unit, an Explorer. 

Hills, mountains, swamps and deserts may conceal valuable minerals. The Explorer prospects these areas, searching for minerals.  Once minerals are located, the Builder can construct a mine. 

In the early part of the game, the most important mineral resource to locate is iron ore.  Processed iron (cast iron) is used by the Builder and the Engineer, and is also used to build military and naval units.

Later in the game, copper, tin, and coal will be important as well. Eventually,  you will send an Explorer to prospect and explore in the New World.
2104:
Welcome to Episode 4, in which you will continue to work with your Builder and Engineer.

Tiles developed by your Builder produce resources each turn. Your Empire gains those resources if the development is connected to the capital city by road. 

There are certain types of resources which are especially important at the beginning of the game.  As you play this and later episodes, keep your Builder and Engineer busy developing and connecting terrain tiles that produce Timber, Iron Ore and Wool, which are important for industry, and Grain and Cattle, which are needed to feed the industrial workers.
2105:
Welcome to Episode 5. You are getting access to the Industry button on the ribbon toolbar.  The Production panel in the Industry Orders screen is used to make materials.

The resources your Empire gains each turn are used to produce materials.  For example, Timber is processed into Lumber, and Iron Ore is converted to Cast Iron.

Lumber and Cast Iron have many uses, for example the Builder uses them for all developments, and the Engineer uses them to build roads.  Wool is turned into Fabric, which is needed to recruit labor and later, to build sailing ships.

Additionally, materials may be sold to other nations for a profit.
2106:
Welcome to Episode 6. You are getting access to a new button on the Industry Orders screen.  

All production of materials requires labor.  As the game progresses your Empire requires more and more labor. The Labor Panel is used to recruit more peasant laborers and to improve the quality of the laborers later in the game.

With the additional Peasant labor, you will be able to make three materials at a time.
2107:
Welcome to Episode 7. You will be putting your Engineer to work in a new activity.

Sometimes resources you need are so far from your capital that the expense and time required for road construction make building a port a better option. Like roads, ports collect resources from any tile on or adjacent to the port’s location. They also collect fish from the ocean and rivers, which helps feed industrial workers.

Since items gathered by a port can move over water, it is not necessary for ports to be connected by road to the capital. If you do eventually connect a port, however, some of the commodities it picks up will move over land.
2108:
Welcome to Episode 8. You are getting access to the Transport button on the ribbon toolbar.  

The roads built by your Engineer have been transporting resources every turn automatically. 
Land (or road) transport is shown with green slider bars on the transport screen.

Unlike road transport, transport of resource by sea (from a port) must have ships assigned to it. The transport screen is used to give these orders.  Each type of commodity that can be moved by water is represented by a blue colored slider bar on the transport screen. 

Use the arrows at the ends of the slider bars to control how much of a commodity your ships will move.
2109:
Welcome to Episode 9. You are gaining control of your navy, and getting access to the Zoom button at the top left of the toolbar.

Your ships are presently all assigned to the home fleet (stationed in the harbor), where they are available for transport orders. In this episode, you will order one ship to move out on the open seas, beginning the exploration of the New World.
2110:
As an Old World ruler, one of your duties is to bring civilization to the tribes of the New World. Of course, if your country makes a few profits at the same time it seems only fair. 

You cannot trade with a Tribe until you have discovered its capital. Tribal capitals along the coast can be discovered by ship. You must send the Explorer to the New World to discover inland capitals.
2111:
Welcome to Episode 11. You are getting access to the Diplomacy button on the ribbon toolbar.  

Diplomatic actions are used to gain influence in other countries without war. This leads to advantages over the other Great Powers when conducting trade. By building a long term peaceful relationship you may eventually convince other countries to join your Empire.
2112:
Welcome to Episode 12. You are getting access to the Trade button on the ribbon toolbar.  

Through trade your Empire makes profits selling materials, and gains additional raw resources from other lands.  As the favored trading partner of a Minor nation, your Great Power gets the first opportunity to buy its products.
2113:
Welcome to Episode 13. You are getting access to the Units button on the Industry Orders screen.  

It’s a good idea to develop defensive forces, and order them to defend each of your provinces. It is especially important to defend the capital. If the capital is conquered, you lose. 

You can build military units,  as well as civilian workers and ships, using the unit building panel in the Industry Orders screen. Consider building a knight or a pikeman.  These are two of the more effective units early in the game.
2114:
Welcome to Episode 14, in which you will prepare an assault force.

Although conquest is not the only viable option for exploiting the New World, the Tribes are a handy target for learning to command an invasion. 

The nations of the Old World tend to be too powerful to be successfully attacked early in the game. However, a small but strong force should be able to conquer a New World province.
2115:
Declaring war is a prerequisite to battle in the Old World. However, the Great Powers play by different rules in the New World,  and no declaration is required.

Overseas invasion is carried out in 2 steps: beachhead and attack. In this episode you will carry out the first step, establishing a beachhead where your troops will land.
2116: As you may recall, overseas invasion is carried out in 2 steps: beachhead and attack. Now that you have established a beachhead, in this episode you will carry out the second step, attacking.
2117:
You’ve conquered a New World province. Now it’s time to learn that there is also another way to benefit from Minor Nations: peacefully buying their land.  

When the Minor Nation sells resources from your land, you will get a cut of the profits.  If you buy the resources, this amounts to a great discount. If the resources are riches, such as gems and diamonds, this will make you a lot of money. 

An important benefit is that once you own land in the New World, other Great Powers cannot attack that province without declaring war on you. This allows you to stake out a province and protect it. (This only applies to the New World.)

Minor Nations start with the tiles around their capitals developed.  Your goal for this episode is to buy one of those developed tiles adjacent to a New World capital. 

Here are the steps you will need to follow: 
1. Use the Explorer to find the capital of a Tribe  you plan to have peaceful relations with.
2. Make a Consulate with that Tribe. 
3. Make an Embassy with that Tribe (Merchant can only buy land  after you have an Embassy).
4. Build a Merchant Unit.
5. Use the Merchant to buy a tile of land adjacent to the Tribal capital.
2118:
When Minor Nations sell resources from land you own, you get a share of the profits. If you are the buyer of the resources, this amounts to a discounted purchase. When other countries buy the resources, the deal brings in net revenue to you. 

The gross revenue from such deals is reported in the Deal Book as Overseas Profits. Someone needs to buy the resources for you to receive these profits. You may need to bid on those resources yourself to realize Overseas Profits and complete this episode.
2119:
Welcome to Episode 19. You are getting access to the Technology button on the ribbon toolbar.  

New technologies increase your abilities and efficiency in every aspect of developing an Empire. As the game progresses, all the Great Powers will research and discover new technologies, attempting to gain advantages over their foes. 

This is the last episode of the tutorial.

• Click the factory button on the toolbar to bring up the Industry Orders screen (it looks like the button in the picture above).

2209:

• Click on the mini-map in the toolbar to quickly scroll from the Old World to the New World.

2211:

1. Choose a Minor Nation to court
2. Establish a trade consulate with that nation
3. Give that nation a trade subsidy
     (more details are given in the Help briefing)

2212:
• Click the coins button on the toolbar to bring up the Trade Orders screen. (It looks like the button in the picture above.)
• Materials are listed at the top of the Trade Orders screen, resources are shown in the bottom half.

• You can find out what resources a Minor Nation sells using the "information" panel on the Diplomacy Orders screen or by investigating the terrain around the capital on the map.
• Click on a "B" to enter a buy bid on the resources sold by the Minor Nation.
• For more help, click on the question mark button.
2213:
• You can reach the Units panel by clicking on the flags icon in the top banner on the Industry Orders screen.
• If you have been playing effectively, all your industrial labor will have been assigned to producing materials. However, because Peasants who are working cannot be drafted into the army or navy, you will need to reduce your materials production orders to make a Peasant available for drafting. 
• Just as each Peasant unit represents a large group of Peasant workers, each military unit constructed represents a regiment.
• For more help, click on the question mark button.
2214:
• You probably don’t have enough labor at the start of this Episode to build 3 Pikemen, and even if you did, you probably don’t have enough labor left over to keep working on industry. You will need to recruit more peasants using the labor panel.
• All units and peasants need to be fed.  As you expand your workforce, it is crucial that you also expand the amount of food (grain, livestock, fish) you are transporting into the city.
• When the unit you built last episode comes up in the unit cycle, give it orders to Defend your capital.
• For more help, click on the question mark button.
2215:
• Fleets must be in a sea zone adjacent to the province to be invaded before the landing site can be established.
• When a group of ships is selected,  a cannon cursor indicates a landing site mission.
• The larger the fleet used, the more land units you can send on the attack next turn.
• To make success more likely, look for a New World province whose force size is shown as two tents, rather than three tents.
• When your Pikemen come up in the unit cycle, just click the ‘No orders this turn’ button. You will use them next turn. 
• For more help, click on the question mark button.
2216:
• Sending your 3 Pikemen on this attack is a good idea.
• When your army comes up in the unit cycle, use the minimap to quickly scroll the map over to the province where you see the invading Fleet at the shore.
• If you previously gave your Pikemen orders to defend, they will not come up automatically in the unit cycle. Click the garrison tents where they are defending to select them. 
• Since the capital city is a port, units encamped there may attack into the overseas province with your landing site.
• To order the attack, hold the cursor over the target province. It will look like a set of crossed swords. Click on the province. A red attack arrow on the map confirms that the attack is ordered.
• The battle will take place after you click the ‘End Turn’ button.
• For more help, click on the question mark button.
2217:
• Use the Units panel in the Industry Orders screen to make a Merchant.
• Use the Treaties panel in the Diplomacy Orders screen to make a Consulate. 
• Once you have the Consulate, make an Embassy with that Tribe.
• Use the Explorer to reveal all the tiles adjacent to the Tribal capital, so you can figure out which one you want to buy.
• It’s important to first buy land in the capital province. If you bought in some other province, then another Great Power could conquer the capital, and you would lose your land.
• Use the online Help for more detailed information about the many wondrous benefits of using the Merchant.
2218:
• Use the hot text or terrain help to confirm which resource is produced in the land you own. Then place a bid on that resource.
• If you bid on the resources and did not receive an offer, the problem is that you used up all your trade cargo holds before that deal came up. You may have to:
1. Refuse other offers --or--
2. Reduce the number of commodities you are selling --or--
3. Dedicate more of your navy to Trade (by reducing Transport orders, or by bringing naval patrols back to your home fleet).
• For more help, click on the question mark button.
2219:
• Click the compass in the ribbon toolbar to bring up the Technology Orders screen.
• Although you can select which technologies to research manually, you should turn on computer control for the technology orders until you are familiar with the game. 
• Successful research is announced at the beginning of a new turn. The exact moment of success is unpredictable.
• While you are waiting for your technology research investments to bear fruit, concentrate on building your transport network, developing more resources, and building up your labor force.   
• For more help, click on the question mark button.
2290:
Sidebar: About Automated Orders

You may delegate many of your responsibilities as monarch to your assistant (also known as the computer).

When this is possible, a button appears on the ribbon at the top left of the screen, which you can toggle between human and computer control. 

Using the assistant is an excellent way to learn. The right way to use it is to click the button so the computer sets the orders, then go in and adjust the orders to achieve your particular short term goals (such as the tutorial episode goals). 

As you become a more experienced ruler, you will find it more efficient to set all orders personally.

2297:

2298:
Clicking this button delegates some of your responsibilities as monarch to your assistant (also known as the computer).

Using the assistant is an excellent way to learn. The right way to use it is to click the button so the computer sets the orders, which gives you an idea of some sensible orders. Then go in and adjust the orders to achieve your particular short term goals (such as the tutorial episode goals). 

If you leave the computer assistant in control, your adjusted orders will be carried out for one turn only, then next turn, the computer assistant will make all new orders. 

So turn the automated assistant off  if you want your changes to be used for more than one turn.
2299:
Welcome to the demo version of Imperialism II: Age of Exploration.

Only the tutorial is available in this version.  The tutorial consists of 19 episodes. In the full version, there is no turn limit on the tutorial, but there is one in this demo version. Even if you haven’t completed the tutorial, the game will end after 85 turns, in the year 1670.
Click the scrolls on the table to begin the tutorial.
3011:
Your civilian units work on the Terrain Map. 

Engineers are used to connect the resources to your transport network so the resources may be used to feed  workers and supply  industries. If a terrain tile is within one tile of a connected road,  port, or the capital city, the resources in that tile are available to the transport network. 

Explorers look for mineral resources and reveal hidden tiles in the New World.
Builders increase the number of resources produced by a terrain tile.
Merchants purchase land from Tribes and Neutral States.
Spies investigate military strength and steal technology.
Railroad workers convert roads to railroads.
3012:
In the toolbar you see a picture of the selected civilian along with information about him. "Selected" means that the particular unit is ready to receive orders.  Orders are given using the four silver button directly under the unit’s name, or by clicking directly on the map. On the map you see your civilian units, a variety of terrain, towns, and  military encampments.

Information about a terrain tile may be seen in the upper right corner of the screen when your cursor is over the tile. You can obtain detailed information about a tile by info-clicking on it. Info-click means a click with the right mouse button, or with the shift key depressed on your keyboard.
3013:
In the Old World you may obtain grain from farm tiles, meat from open range and water tiles,  wool from fertile hills, horses from horse corrals, and timber from dense and scrub forest tiles. You may find iron ore and copper in the hills or mountains, and tin in the swamps. All these items are called resources.

Early in the game you should rapidly increase the amount of these resources available to your workers and industry.  

Your explorer can search for hidden mineral resources. Your builder can construct developments on  terrain tiles so that the tile will produce resources for your Empire. Your engineer can build roads so that they are on the same tile with resources or adjacent to them. This allows any resources from the tile to be transported and used.
3014:
As you move your cursor across the map it will alter according to what will happen if you click in that location. Often this will be information about  what will happen if you send your civilian to that terrain tile. You can safely experiment because any order you give can be canceled at no cost. 

An "eye" means the explorer  will search the tile for minerals.
A "hammer" means the builder will build a development , the engineer will build a port or fort, or the spy will begin gathering information.
A "green arrow" means the civilian moves to the tile but performs no work this turn.
"Gold coins" means the merchant will buy the land.
A "road" means the engineer will construct a road from his present tile into the tile where you click.

A civilian unit who is working on a project animates. A question mark cursor appears when you place the mouse over a working unit. Click on the unit and a dialog box informs you what he is doing and lets you cancel or confirm the orders.
3015:
Each of your available units is presented for orders in turn. This is called the units cycle. The unit that is active at any point in the units cycle is called the selected unit. 

If you wish to select a civilian unit without waiting for it in the cycle, move the cursor over a unit on the map. When the cursor becomes a small hammer with a flag, click to select the unit. 

This allows you to select units that are not currently in the automatic cycle, or to command units in a different order than presented by the cycle.
3016:
Resources:
Wool: make Fabric
Cotton: make Fabric
Timber: make Lumber
Tin:  (together with Copper) make Bronze 
Copper:  (together with Tin) make Bronze
Iron Ore: make Cast Iron, (together with Coal) make Steel
Coal: (together with Iron Ore) make Steel
Sugar Cane: make Refined Sugar
Tobacco: make Cigars
Fur: make Fur Hats

Horses:  build military units

Materials:
Fabric:  recruit Peasants, build ships, build military units
Lumber:  build military units, build ships, Builder build developments, Engineer build roads, ports and forts, Rail Builder build rail
Paper:  build civilian units, train laborers
Bronze: build military units, build Ships, level 1 and 2 forts
Cast Iron: build military units, build Ships, Builder build developments, Engineer build roads and ports
Steel: build military units, build Ships, level 3 forts, Rail Builder build rail

Luxuries:
(on the Simple Economy game variant, any worker will consume any luxury. On the Complex Economy game variant)
Refined Sugar: required by Apprentice Workers
Cigars: required by Journeyman Workers
Fur Hats: required by Master Workers


Food:
(on the Simple Economy game variant, population will consume any food. On the Complex Economy game variant, population requires a balanced diet)
Grain: required by all laborers, military units and ships
Fish and Meat: required by all laborers, military units and ships (Fish and Meat are interchangeable)
3021:
The selected unit may be commanded from the toolbar or by  clicking on the map directly. On the toolbar  four buttons under the name of the selected unit allow you to:

Disband a civilian unit (unit icon with arrow pointing down)
Since this decision is final you will be asked to confirm it.

Cycle to the next unit (unit icon with arrow pointing to the right)
Use this command if you want to give the unit an order later in the turn.

End the turn of the selected unit (unit icon with exclamation point)
The unit will be available next turn.

Put the selected unit to sleep (unit icon with letter z)
The unit will be removed from the unit cycle until you select it manually on the map.
3022:
Civilian units are depicted in three ways on the map. 

An animating unit is working on a project. These units will stop animating and return to the units cycle when the project is completed.

A unit flashing with a white outline is the selected unit. Orders you give pertain to this unit.

A gray scale unit has been put to sleep or given other orders that end his turn.
3023:
Improvements such as roads, railroads, forts, and ports as well as increases to the production of a terrain tile are all paid for with materials. These improvements are built by three civilian units, the Builder, the Engineer, and the Railroad Worker.

Roads can be built in any type of terrain.
Railroads can eventually be built in any terrain, but more difficult terrain requires more advanced technology.
Ports can be built in any terrain except hills or mountains.  A port must be on a river or adjacent to the ocean.
Forts are built only in tiles that contain a town or a capital city.

In the toolbar display when one of these units is selected you see a tally of available materials for construction, and a table listing the costs of the improvements the selected unit can build.

Construction always requires lumber and a metal in equal amounts. The type of metal (bronze, cast iron, or steel) and the amount of lumber and metal required depend on the type of construction.
3024:
Transport, industry, trade,  diplomacy, and technology screens do not need to be visited every turn. When something in the world situation has changed, you will need to change your orders on one or more of these screens. Generally, the industry screen requires the most attention of the five. 

To reach one of  these screens, click on one of the icons on the gold ribbon at the bottom of the screen.  Often the orders screens can be managed by your computer advisor.
3025:
There are several useful shortcuts for navigating on the map without scrolling across your nation or the world. 

The mini-map in the upper right portion of the toolbar permits you to jump to any part of the world. This is useful for moving civilians, military, and naval units.  

The magnifying glass button at the upper left corner of the toolbar allows you to see more of the world at once. This is often useful when moving fleets through large sea zones.

Clicking on a civilian unit in the toolbar centers the map on that civilian. Typing ‘C’ centers the map on the selected unit, or on your capital if no unit is selected. 

Finally, your Explorer unit can be ordered to jump to a particular type of terrain to explore or prospect by clicking on one of the icons displayed  in the toolbar when the explorer is selected.
3026:
Click on the Status and Reports button  on the top of the toolbar to bring up a list of status reports. That list shows a Civilian Roster, an Army Roster and a Navy Roster. Each Roster shows a list of all your units in that category. You can click on a unit in the roster to close the roster and center the map over that unit. 

There is also a Development Roster which shows a list of all the tiles you have developed with the Builder. 

These rosters are useful for quickly checking on whether any units or developments should be upgraded. The keyboard shortcuts to them are: F9 Development Roster, F10 Army Roster, F11 Navy Roster, and F12 Civilian Roster.
3031:
This screen represents the industrial might of your Empire. Here you order production, using the labor of workers to produce raw resources into materials such as cast iron or lumber, manage your labor force, and build new units for use on the terrain map.

Use the gold banner at the top of the Industry screen to:

Go to the production panel with the gear icon
Go to the unit construction panel with the flags icon
Go to the labor panel with the hammer icon
3032:
The blue banner at the top of the production screen is called the warehouse. It lists all the resources and commodities your nation has this turn. 

If you are not sure which resource or material an icon represents, place the mouse over the icon and read the text on the gold banner in the upper right portion of the screen.

When you end your turn, resources you have connected to your capital city on the map are moved into the warehouse for use on the next turn. Materials you make on this screen are added to the warehouse for next turn as well.
3033:
Each of the production sliders uses different resources, but all sliders need two units of resources for every material produced.  Concentrate on cast iron, lumber, and fabric to rapidly expand your Empire’s infrastructure early in the game.

To use a slider to make a material, click on the gold arrow at the right end of the slider. The slider bar changes color confirming the production order. You may also click within the slider bar to increase or decrease production. The resources are deducted when the orders are given, but the new material is not ready until the next turn. 

To reduce an order for production click on the gold arrow to the left end of the slider. The resources are returned to the warehouse. You can change your mind about what to produce as often as you like. Production orders are not final until you end your turn.

You may choose to assign your production to the computer using the button at the top left of the screen. The sliders will be filled in automatically.  There is no guarantee that the computer will share all your short term goals.
3034:
Early in the game, your most urgent needs are cast iron and lumber for development, and fabric for recruiting additional labor. Try to balance production between these three commodities. Try to develop sources for of the raw materials (timber, iron ore, and wool) that are required to produce a steady supply of these necessary materials.

If you find your country is short of needed resources you should try to acquire them through trade.
3035:
To reach the labor panel of the industry screen select the hand with hammer icon at the top of the screen.

On the labor panel peasants are recruited by spending fabric. Click on the arrow at the right end of the slider to recruit more peasants. Each peasant eats one unit of food every turn (grain or meat) and if your population outpaces your food resources, the peasants will eventually starve.

On the right side of the screen are icons representing grain and meat. Everyone in your population eats one grain or one meat every turn. Place your cursor over the gain or meat icons. The hot text at the top right of the screen shows how many units you are transporting in each turn. 

Your population consists of  each industrial worker, each unit in the army, and each naval unit. In the lower left portion of the labor screen you see three boxes labeled population. The total population in these boxes equals the total amount of meat and grain eaten each turn.  Unless you have huge food stockpiles in the warehouse, it is important to keep your level of food transport greater than or equal to level of food consumption. 

On the labor panel  additional sliders  become available later in the game.  These sliders are used for improving your work force through training. Peasants produce only one unit of labor per person but training increases this number, making your work force much more efficient.
3036:
To reach the units panel of the industry screen select the crossed flags icon on the banner at the top of the screen.

All military and naval units require a peasant laborer. Like workers in industry, each military or naval unit eats food each turn. If you build too many units too quickly, your industry will not have enough labor to continue to develop.

To build a unit, select the unit by clicking on its picture in one of the panels on the right side of the screen. The selected unit appears in the large box on the left side of the screen and the text provides information about it.

In the middle of this build panel are icons and numbers which tell you the cost of the unit. When you lack the necessary amount of a commodity it is shown with a red x superimposed. Above the costs you see two gold arrows and a small text box.

Click the right arrow to increase the number you are building, and the left arrow to decrease. The number you have ordered appears in the text box and near the unit picture on the right side of the screen. All units take one turn to build and are available for action next turn.
3037:
Early in the game over-construction of military forces slows your growth significantly.  This is due to the fact that your food supplies are limited. If military and naval units are eating most of your food, you will not be able to recruit enough labor to expand rapidly. Generally,  a good balance is obtained by limiting your combined population of military and naval units to less than or equal to the population of laborers for industry.  These numbers can be compared using the population chart in the lower  left corner of the labor panel.

Civilian units do not eat food and so may be constructed more freely. If you have excess cast iron and lumber production early in the game, you should probably construct more builders and engineers. If the civilians you already own are sometimes idle due to lack of materials, new construction of these types will not help. Remember that spies and explorers operate at no cost to you once constructed.   If more of these units seem useful, go ahead and build them.
3038:
Early in the game you can build few units due to your low food supplies, so build units with specific tasks in mind.

To attack tribes and obtain land in the New World build Knights and Pikemen. To defend provinces you take invest your bronze in forts, not additional units.

To attack forts build light infantry and light artillery. The earliest units of any use in these categories are calivermen and horse-artillery. Both must be researched. It is difficult to attack forts at all until you have at least three units of horse-artillery.

To defend fortified provinces, once your foes have developed light artillery, build additional heavy artillery. This way you will out range the attacking artillery by more. Artillery is also necessary to defend non-fortified provinces, but in these situations you should build infantry or cavalry to protect it. 

In the final era of the game, sharpshooters, rifle infantry, and guards infantry are all effective on both attack and defense.
3039:
New naval construction may be based on the need for additional transport and trade capacity or on the need for a fleet during times of war.  All ships you build appear on the terrain map in your Home Fleet. As long as they remain there they can be used to conduct trade and transport.

In most games, the best strategy is to build no ships until you can build galleons. Galleons may be built once your Empire learns the technology of convoying.  Unlike vessels developed later galleons are both powerful in battle (during their era) and can carry significant amounts of cargo.  This makes them the ideal ship when you have little extra food to feed a large navy.

Small warships, like the sloop or the frigate, are useful mainly for attacking and patrolling. They should not be built to carry cargo because their small capacity makes this a waste of your population.

Later in the game, you will have sufficient food supplies and population to specialize your naval forces. Slow large ships like Indiamen may be built to carry cargo, while your galleon fleet can be upgraded to a powerful squadron of Ships of the Line.
3041: There are four pages to the customizing screen, and you may page through them using the red arrows in the lower corner of each page. To return to the map room click on the Return Arrow found on the candle to the left of the screen.
3042:
Under the heading Difficulty Settings on the first page you see two economic settings that can be either "Simple" or "Complex". If you play on Easy or Introductory settings these are set to "Simple" automatically. The AI plays the same way regardless of these settings so, for the most part, "Simple" setting only makes it easier for the human players in the game.

"Simple" means that any food will satisfy a food demand or that any luxury will satisfy a luxury demand. This makes it much easier to keep your labor force fed and happy during the game. It means you don't have to worry as much about creating an Empire with access to diverse commodities. The "Complex" setting means that a worker who demands a particular food or luxury must receive that exact item or he won't do any work.

Even on the "Complex" setting workers never die if given the wrong food or luxury. They merely perform no work that turn. On both simple and complex settings workers eventually starve if they are not fed any food at all.
3043:
Generally, categories on the customizing screen which include five levels directly affect difficulty of your game.

The five settings found in each of these categories correspond to the five difficulty settings available in the Map Room. For instance, if you play on normal setting  all of these categories are set to normal. Normal means no advantages to either computer or human.

Consult your Imperialism II manual for more information on these difficulty settings.
3044:
Unlike the difficulty levels many of the game play options or game variants do not affect the difficulty of the game directly.

Use these variant settings to decide what kind of a world you would like to play in, not how difficult the game will be. The most significant choice you can make is to play a "development" game or an "aggressive" game. 

In the development game the computer players are very unwilling to attack. You will be free to develop your Empire as you like.

In the aggressive game wars will be frequent and diplomatic solutions very rarely tried by the computer players. 

Consult your Imperialism II manual for more information on game variants.
3051:
On the bid and offers screen you tell your merchants which commodities to try to buy and sell when the world market convenes after the end of the turn. 

There are no guarantees on the world market. Your empire might need iron, for example, and have plenty of money, but if no other country is offering iron you will not be able to buy any. Likewise if no other country is bidding on the commodities you offer, you will not be able to sell them.

Use your powerful industries to take advantage of the minor nations: buy their cheap raw resources and sell them back expensive materials 

Consider changing the bids entered if there is something in particular you wish to buy. You should decide what to attempt to buy based on what resources you lack.
3052:
Each commodity traded on the market is pictured to the left of the screen. At the top of the column are  materials with resources beneath them. 

Hot text will remind you of each commodity's name. Information on the screen includes the current world price and the amount you have available in your warehouse.  The same warehouse is used for industry and trade.

The numbers  to the right under the large ship display the division of your ship’s cargo holds. Cargo holds assigned to trade may be used to deliver commodities you offer and to pick up commodities you bid on.  With rare exceptions, you are unable to buy and sell more total items in one turn than the number of cargo hold you assign to trade. 

To change the allocation of cargo holds, making more shipping available for trade, you can:  move ships on the high seas to your home port; build more ships on the industry screen; or reduce the number of cargo holds being used for transport on the transport screen.
3053:
At the beginning of the game you should immediately begin to buy commodities, especially resources your Empire lacks.  You should sell commodities when you need money and when you can afford to expend your valuable materials in this way.  All the materials your industry can produce can be used either to assist your development or sold to make money.

An attempt to buy a commodity is called a bid. To bid, click on a "B" icon in the bids column.  A gold wax seal confirms your  action.  You are limited to three bids in any turn until the technology of trade fairs is discovered by your Empire. Additionally, if you decide to offer something for sale, you will not be able to bid on the same item in the same turn. 

An attempt to sell a commodity is called an offer.  To offer, click on an "O" icon in the offers column. A red seal confirms your action. Enter the maximum quantity you are willing to sell using the slider that appears. You can offer for sale anything that you have, unless you have insufficient cargo holds to make the delivery. You cannot offer and bid on the same commodity on the same turn.

Once you set your offers and bids, you need to return to this screen only if you want to change them.
3054:
The sliders that appear on the bid an offers screen when you click on the offer "O" icon, establish the maximum amount you are willing to sell. When you end your turn, that amount is offered to any country that bid on that commodity until it is all sold.

To reduce the time spent changing your orders on the bid and offers screen, it may be a good idea to establish a set amount of  a material that you are willing to sell each turn. For instance if you produce three fabric per turn on the industry screen, you could set your  offer slider for fabric to offer for sale one or two units every turn.  As long as there is a supply of fabric, this offer will be made each turn with no further orders from you.
3055:
Your computer advisor for trade is activated by clicking on the human face icon at the upper left part of the screen. The icon changes to a computer confirming that you have given control of trade to your advisor.  You regain control by clicking on the button again.

One good way to learn about trade is to turn on the advisor temporarily to see what the computer would choose to do. Then you can restore human control and make any changes to the computer’s orders you feel are necessary. 

Often, on the first turn of the game, the computer will choose not to bid or offer anything.  Because your Empire has no trade consulates with Neutral States, and because your warehouse is fairly well supplied, the computer sees no reason to conduct trade.  You might want to trade on the first turn if you can look further ahead  than your advisor and see upcoming shortages. 

Once you establish trading relations with Neutral States or Tribes, or once you begin expending the commodities in the warehouse, your computer advisor will enter bids and offers if you give it control of trade.
3056:
Although your Empire usually begins the game with plentiful cash on hand, this is often expended in a few turns. Eventually you need to place your finances on permanently sound footing by making a profit. Selling materials is always more profitable than selling resources. Anything produced by industry is considered a material.

The best material to offer for sale depends on your Empire’s current needs and may change turn by turn especially at the beginning of the game.  Although, like all  materials, fabric is  needed for expansion and development, it is often the best choice for selling early in the game.  Most Great Powers are able to make fabric at an early date, and it is not as much in demand  for development as are lumber and cast iron.

Using your computer advisor to make the choice is sometimes a good idea.  However,  your advisor does not know the details of your planning. For instance if you are saving fabric to recruit  labor in a few turns, your advisor just sees a large stockpile of fabric available for selling.

As your Empire develops, your industries will begin producing extra materials. Then you can offer a variety of materials for sale every turn.
3057:
Successful manipulation of the economy  depends on overcoming shortages. Using both transport and trade,  you must establish a balanced supply (of at least two units per turn) of timber, wool, and iron ore for the early development of your Empire . You should bid on resources that you cannot obtain in your country, either because you have not found them or because your builders and engineers have not connected them yet.

Once you have supplies of the three basic resources, work toward reliable sources (one unit per turn) of both copper and tin. Again, use trade bids to fill needs that your local resources do not meet.

When these early goals are met, you should begin to expand in both the New World and the Old World. This expansion involves transporting riches or rare products from the New World.  Your trade bids will again have to be used to meet needs that cannot be obtained through transport.
3058:
The number of cargo holds assigned to trade establishes the maximum amount of any single commodity that you can offer for sale. Normally, however, the more important restriction on trade is the fact that each cargo hold can be used but once per turn.

The rule for the use of cargo holds is that the buying country picks up the commodities if that country  is a Great Power. If the country is not a Great Power, the selling country is responsible for delivery. 

If your cargo holds are all used delivering materials you sell to Neutral States or Tribes, you will be unable to accept the offers to buy which come from other countries because you will have no free cargo holds to pick up the commodities. 

Additionally, since commodities are always offered and accepted in the same predictable order, it is possible and often necessary to reserve cargo holds for offers that arrive later. For instance if you bid on wool and iron ore, but use all your cargo holds picking up wool, you would not be able to pick up any iron.  This means you might decide to reject some offers of wool in order to reserve cargo holds for iron ore
3059:
The prices listed on the bid and offers screen are last turn’s prices These are all recalculated every turn when all countries have entered bids and offers and ended their turns. If demand outstrips supply, the price rises. If there is a glut, the price falls.  Radical changes are unlikely. Generally, last turn’s price is close to the new price once the bids and offers of all the countries are compared.

After a new price is set for each commodity, the bids and offers of all the countries in the game are used to create a list of all potential deals for this turn.  Bids on each commodity are ranked for each offering country in an order which is determined by the price the bidder would pay, and the strength of the diplomatic relations between the offering country and the bidding country. You can offer to pay extra (above the world price) using the diplomacy screen.  

Potential deals are presented one at a time in order to each potential buyer.  Items from an offering nation are offered to their first place bidder, followed (if any remain unsold) by an offer to their second place bidder, and so on.

Your country participates in this process if you decided to bid on commodities and if another nation offers the commodities to you.  These commodity offers are presented after you end your turn and before the new turn begins.
3071:
The Diplomacy screen may be used to learn about and interact with other Great Powers, Tribes, and Neutral states.
 
Click on one of the five icons at the top of the screen to select among different types of diplomatic activity on five different panels.

Click on the first icon a yellow "i" on the left,  to obtain information about the other countries in the game.

Click on one of the next three icons at the top of the screen to take diplomatic actions. You make diplomatic overtures such as embassies, consulates, and pacts, provide grants to the leaders of other countries, and set trade policies using one of these three icons. 

Click on the icon on the far right  to find out the victory condition for the game and the current score. Victory is always obtained by control of the Old World. The number of provinces required depends on how many provinces there are. Usually, the winning total is around 30 provinces.
3072:
Although there will eventually be a large number of  diplomatic options, at the beginning of the game your actual options are limited.  

Use the face button at the top left of the screen to turn diplomacy over to your computer advisor.  You can use this function to see what the computer would do, then restore personal control and make any changes you wish.

As a first step, use the information "I" icon to look at the various Neutral States in the Old World. You are looking for information about what resources these countries export, as well as the levels of friendliness each one feels towards your country and the other Great Powers. At the beginning of the game these diplomatic relationships are always fairly even.  For help using the information panel click on the help topic "Obtaining information".

Once you have information about these Neutral States consider establishing a trade consulate in one or more of them. Choose Neutral States that export products you may need. Trade consulates are considered a diplomatic overture, and are established using the Overtures panel.  For help using the Overtures panel click on the help topic "Diplomatic Overtures".

Once a new trade consulate is established in a neutral state, each completed trade deal between your Empire and this country causes an improvement of your diplomatic relationship.  Eventually, their leaders could decide to join your Empire peacefully.  Consulates also allow you to set trade polices to encourage more trade.
3073:
Click on the yellow ‘i" icon at the upper left part of the screen to reach the information panel. No actions can be taken using this panel. Here you obtain different sorts of information by clicking on any country on the map.

There are four small icons in the center of the upper part of the screen. Each of these icons provides access to different information about any country you click on : 

The top icon (an "i") provides basic information about any country.
The  second icon (a small scroll) provides information about diplomatic status such as treaties and wars.
The third icon (a small document) provides information about  relationships,--a measure of hostility or friendliness.
The fourth icon (coins) provides information about trade and exports.

To obtain any particular fact, two clicks may be required. One click to choose among the four icons--the type of information sought; and a second click on the map to choose the country that you are interested in.  

Alternatively, if you are interested particular facts (such as exports, or relationships) of several countries,  select the appropriate icon first, and then click on the countries on the map in succession.
3074:
To make diplomatic overtures to other countries, click on the scrolls icon at the top of the screen. This takes you to the overtures panel.

To make a diplomatic overture, first select one of the large scrolls on the panel, then click on the country  you select for the overture. A small  overture symbol appears on the map within the borders of that country.  At the beginning of the game trade consulates are most useful.

Because you already have embassies with Great Powers, you cannot establish trade consulates with them. Embassies include trade consulates within them. The ability to establish embassies with Neutral States and the Tribes you discover is obtained by researching  the diplomatic expertise technology. 

You can always declare war on any Old World country.   It is not necessary to declare war on Tribes.

If you want to cancel an overture click on the icon that appears in that nation. It will disappear. Nothing is final until you end your turn. Overtures you make this turn take effect next turn. Some overtures may be refused by other nations, but trade consulates and declarations of war cannot be refused.
3075:
To make grants of money to other countries, click on the document icon at the top of the screen. This takes you to the grants and relationships panel.

To make a grant first select one of the large certificates (without a lock) on the panel, then click on the country  you select for the grant.  A small  grant symbol appears on the map within the borders of that country.  To set a grant that will occur every turn with no action from you, use the certificates with the locks on them.

At the beginning of the game grants are not a good idea because there are more urgent requirements for your money. You cannot make a grant until you have an embassy in the other country.

Any grant improves the relationship between the granting country and the recipient. The larger the grant, the more the relationship improves.  Generally, grants improve relations more than trade deals, and several small grants over time improve relations more than a single large grant.

The map on this panel always displays the relationships of your Empire. When any other country reaches a dark green color on this map it means that country might accept an offer to join your Empire peacefully. This overture is made using the overtures panel.

If you want to cancel an grant click on the icon that appears in that nation. It will disappear. Nothing is final until you end your turn.
3076:
Click on the coin icon at the top of the screen to reach the trade policies panel.  

A trade subsidy provides a percent change to the world price on all commodities traded with the selected country. If you are selling to that country, the percent change will reduce the price. If you are buying, the price you pay will increase. 

Using subsidies you can become the favored trading nation of a valuable Neutral State or Tribe even if some other Great Power has more friendly relations with them. This guarantees your traders the right to purchase the exports of the Neutral State or Tribe first.  Each trade improves the relations between the two countries.

Select the amount of the subsidy you wish to provide by clicking on one of the coins. Then click on the nation you wish to subsidize. You see a small icon confirming the subsidy. To cancel the subsidy, click on this icon.  

To provide a subsidy that will make your Great Power the favored trading nation of the recipient, select the 5% subsidy and hold down the control key when you click on the receiving country. The amount of the subsidy will be established at the minimum level to put your Empire in first place.

Boycotts prevent all trade between the two countries. Colony boycotts forbid your New World colonies from trading with the recipient, but do not prohibit your home country from doing so.

Your Empire must first establish trade consulates with Tribes and Neutral States (using the overtures panel) before you can set trade polices with those nations using this panel.
3077:
Generally, select a few minor nations for diplomatic action. They should produce resources you are interested in, and offer useful geographical advantages for your long range plans. 

Rapidly establish trade consulates and embassies in these nations, and try to maintain friendly relations with other nations that these selected nations like. If you start a war, do so far away from your trading partners.

Your goal is to become the favorite great power of a minor nation. Once you are the favorite great power, you have a good chance of eventual peaceful control of their country.
3081:
Technological research represents both new inventions, such as the cotton gin, as well as increased knowledge in other fields such as diplomacy or finance.  For convenience all these developments are termed "technologies". 

As new technologies are discovered by your Empire, more choices for new research projects appear.  As ruler, you decide which developments should be researched next. Your researchers can work on a limited number of projects at one time (three or four) .  You decide what technology should be researched in each of these research slots.

Your Empire, and the empires of your foes,  progress through seven technological eras in a full game. Technologies in later eras may depend on several earlier developments.

To obtain a new technology that no other country has discovered, money must be spent. The minimum per turn cost of research increases $100 per turn for each era. An era one technology costs at least $100 per turn to research, while an era seven technology costs at least $700 per turn.  

However, if other countries have already discovered a technology, your Empire can eventually learn it for free.  To do this, the technology sought must still be placed in one of your research slots, but money need not be spent. The rate at which you gain the technologies of other countries can be greatly increased by using spies.

Be sure to take advantage of your computer advisor if you are not sure how to proceed. The advisor will supply a short term goal and a direction to your research.
3082:
To select technologies by type the six filter buttons above the scroll on the right hand side of the screen are used. By clicking on the button labeled "navy" for instance you filter out all technologies except those related to your navy.

Use the three medallions to the side of the right hand scroll to display technologies according to whether you already know them or not.  The top medallion displays technology your Empire already knows. The middle medallion displays technology that can currently be researched if you have a vacant research slot. The lower medallion displays technologies that can be picked as goals. Generally, goals are technologies that you cannot learn about right away, but supply a direction for your current research. 

The six filter buttons work the same way regardless of which medallion you select.  For instance, the army filter shows you army-related technology that you already know,  or that you could research, or that could be set as a goal, depending on which medallion you select.

You may click on the small magnifying glass button that appears with each technology to obtain more detail about that development. This can be used to see where a technology will lead you in the future.
3083:
A new project is started by moving a listed "researchable" technology from the right side of the screen to one of the open available slots on the left side of the screen.

First,  to see a list of all your researchable technologies, make sure that the middle of the three gold medallions is highlighted in white. This medallion lists the technology currently available for research on the right side of the screen.  Also make sure that the "show all" filter button above the listed technologies is selected. 

Pick a technology to research from this list. Click on the compass button next to the text describing the technology. One of your available slots on the left side is filled with your selection.

Now you may allocate additional cash to the project using the slider in that slot. The more cash spent, the faster you will gain the benefits of the new technology.
3084:
When a project is canceled all cash spent so far is lost. It is not applied to a newly selected project.

Click on the skull button in the slot of the unwanted project. The slot becomes available. You will be asked to confirm, if you have already spent cash on the project. No confirmation is necessary when you change your mind about a project on the same turn in which you began it.
3085:
Turn control of research over to your computer advisor by clicking on the button in the gold ribbon on the top left part of the screen.

If you turn control of the technology screen over to the computer it will establish a long-term research goal for you and fill in all of your open slots. It will also allocate cash each turn.

One good way to play, especially for beginners, is to allow the computer to pick the projects.  Once this is done,  you can take control back by clicking on the computer button. Now you have control of the cash to be spent on each project.
3086:
Click on the third of the three medallions next to the scroll (nearest the bottom of the screen). 
This lists all projects available as long-tern goals. From this list, choose a goal and click on its target icon. The technology will appear in the goal slot at the top left part of the screen.

Next, click on the middle medallion. Technologies that lead to your goal are listed at the top highlighted with green text. You can now fill as many slots as desired with technologies that lead to your goal. Of course, sometimes only one technology is available that will lead to the goal you picked.

Use the arrows in each research slot  to allocate per turn spending to each of the selected projects.
3087:
When other Great Powers already have a technology, a little flag with their country color appears in the description of that technology.  You have an increased chance of learning a new technology that another country already knows about. In fact, when other countries have previously researched a technology successfully, you may put that technology in a research slot, put no money in, and still eventually learn the new technology.

Your chances of stealing the knowledge of other nations in this way vastly increases if you have a spy in a country who has a technology you are researching. If you do place a spy, the flags will be marked with a tiny "s".
3121:
You have ended your turn and the world market is now open. You now receive offers from nations selling the types of commodities that you tried to buy on the bid and offers screen. 

After each offer is acted upon by you (the potential buyer) any commodities in that offer remaining unpurchased are passed on to other nations that bid on those commodities.

Of course you might not be the first buyer in line. The offers you see may already have been passed up by other nations acting ahead of you.
3122:
The offer sheet appears in the center of the screen. It provides simple information on the current offer. 

To obtain more information about the market, click on the small commodity icons on the markets scroll on the right side of the screen. As the icon is selected the scroll opens to  display  details on the world market in that commodity. 

The left side of the scroll lists the nations offering to sell the commodity and the quantity each one is offering. The row of small flags beneath the offering nation’s name shows the order in which the nation will offer the commodity to the various bidders.

On the right page is a list of bidding nations with the amount of cargo holds each currently has available. A Great Power with no remaining cargo holds cannot accept any deals regardless of their position in line.
3123:
Information about the current offer is provided to the left of the offer sheet.  There are two reasons to accept an offer. Either the offer serves a diplomatic purpose--meaning that acceptance improves the relationship of the offering and purchasing nations; or the offer fulfills a need of your warehouse. The most useful offers achieve both these goals.

In order to gain the diplomatic benefits of trading, you must open a trade consulate in the other nation during your turn (before trade offers are made).  If you decide to accept a deal only for diplomatic gain, there is no reason to purchase more than 1 unit of the commodity. The fact that a deal is made supplies the benefit, the quantity purchased is irrelevant.

In cases where your warehouse actually needs the commodity you should be guided by your actual needs and the number of cargo holds you have remaining for trade this turn.
3124:
The trade book is an informational tool. The only orders you can give on this screen are contained on the offer sheet itself. 

As each offer is presented, you can accept any number up to the amount offered, as long as you have cargo holds available to pick up the items. Change the number in the box and then click the accept seal shown on the offer sheet. To reject a deal, click on the reject seal. 

If you decide that you have purchased enough cotton, for example, check the box "done buying this commodity". You will be presented with no more cotton offers this turn.
3125:
Each turn, it is important to use your limited cargo holds wisely.  As each offer is accepted, the number of cargo holds remaining this turn goes down, as displayed by the number near the ship icon.

Commodities are always traded in the order shown on the bid and offers screen and in the icon list on the markets scroll.

This means that if you desperately need iron, for example, you may need to stop accepting all the wool you can get, to reserve some of your limited cargo holds for the iron coming later. In this case,  you should use the trade scroll (iron icon) to look at the market in iron. If one of the nations selling iron shows your flag as its top bidder, you will definitely receive an iron offer this turn. You should save some cargo holds  for it.
3131:
The transport screen is used to display the totals of all the materials and resources anywhere in your Empire that are available for movement so they can be used for production or trade. Since your capital city represents your national industry and your national trading center,  it is necessary to move resources and materials to the capital in order to use them.

Transport always refers only to commodities moved within the bounds of your Empire: the land you control that appears in your country’s color on the diplomacy map. Commodities brought from other countries are moved using trade on the bid and offers screen.

All the resources and materials shown on this screen are "connected". This term means that they are included within a land and sea network that is capable of moving them to the capital.  As your civilian units build more roads, ports, and developments on the terrain map, more resources and materials will be connected.
3132:
At the beginning of the game,  your Empire’s transport network consists only of the commodities immediately adjacent to your capital city. Using builders to increase the production of terrain tiles, and engineers to build roads, you can connect more commodities to your capital by roads. All commodities you connect by road will appear on the transport screen within a green slider representing transport by land. 

As you expand by building ports either in your own country or overseas, the commodities will be connected by water transport with a blue slider on the transport screen. Unlike land transport, water transport requires cargo holds for transport. 

Consider the needs of industry, and the resources already available (as displayed on the transport screen) when planning the next task of your engineer or builder.  Whenever possible, site new roads and ports so that  the adjacent tiles include several commodities that you will find useful.
3133:
Each slider that appears on the screen represents the maximum amount your Empire can transport of a single commodity.  As new commodities are connected, more sliders appear on the screen. Place your mouse cursor over a commodity icon. the text in the upper right corner of the screen lets you know what that commodity is, and how much of it you have in your warehouse .

The scroll on the left side of the screen displays the demands of your industrial workers. At the beginning of the game, these demands are for food. Later, when some of your workers are more highly trained, they will demand consumer goods represented as refined sugar, cigars, and fur hats.

You can compare the amount of a commodity being demanded with the amount you are transporting on this screen.  A transport shortage may not be an immediate problem if your warehouse has a plentiful surplus. Additionally, consumer good demands may be met by industrial production and trade as well as transport.

The scroll on the right side displays the number of cargo hold in your entire fleet and breaks these down according to whether they are assigned to sea transport on this screen, available for trading, or outside the home port as part of the navy.
3134:
At the beginning of the game you do not need to give any orders on this screen since your land transport occurs automatically each turn. The sliders representing land transport are color coded with green bars.  The green (land) transport is included on the screen only so you can see how many units of each commodity you are receiving. 

Once you build or conquer your first port , you will see blue color-coded sliders representing water transport.  Commodities that are moved by water at any portion of their journey to your capital are displayed as blue.

To see what your computer advisor would do with this water transport, click on the human face in the upper left part of the screen.  The icon changes to a computer and the transport screen is set to computer control. You may choose to leave the screen this way, or restore human control and make changes in the orders entered by the computer.

To increase or decrease your water transport manually, click on the gold arrows to either side of a slider that is all blue or has some blue in it.   Alternatively you may click within the slider bar.
3135:
Early in the game, your Empire’s most immediate needs will be grain, livestock, and fish.  Each of your industrial workers, military units, and ships must eat one unit of one of these commodities every turn.  If units are not fed, they will eventually starve to death.

Together grain, meat, and fish are considered food. Food does not appear on the trade screen and cannot be purchased on the world market. This means that your transport network and the orders you give on the transport screen must feed your entire population each turn.
