Sometimes when you start a new game it may take several turns before your Empire can feed everyone reliably.  The amount of food you receive each turn at the start of the game depends on the quality of your capital city site and on the difficulty setting you choose.

In most cases it will be possible to use the stockpiled food in your warehouse to feed your population while your builders and engineers expand the transport network. In rare cases you may want to disband military units to avoid starvation of you industrial workers.  If a unit of population starves, it will be taken first from industry. This is dangerous at the beginning of the game because only consistent production from industry can get your development off to a fast start.
3136:
As you change your transport orders look at the information under the ship icon on the right side of the transport screen. The ship represents the total number of cargo holds in all the ships your Empire owns. Each cargo hold can be used for only one item each turn.

You see that as transport orders are increased cargo holds are moved from the trade number and allocated to the transport number. If you reduce transport orders more cargo holds are allocated to trade. 

If you run out of cargo holds you will not be able to transport more commodities by water and you will have to select those commodities you want to receive.  

Generally, if you have available resources or materials to transport, and unused labor on your industry screen, you should construct additional vessels for your home fleet in order to make use of all the commodities in your Empire’s transport network.
3137:
Once you enter a war some of your sea transport may become endangered. This is shown on the transport screen by an orange colored slider. Endangered commodities may be intercepted by hostile fleets when you end your turn. 

Commodities are shown as endangered if there are any hostile ships patrolling or blockading outside the port the commodities originate from or outside the destination capital city port. You may choose to risk the interception of these endangered commodities or reduce your sea transport orders to avoid it. 

The overall speed and strength of your home fleet influences whether endangered commodities are in fact intercepted, and whether the fleet can defend itself if the interception does occur. 

You can also station patrolling fleets in the sea zones outside your ports to fight or drive away the intercepting enemy ships.
3161:
This screen appears whenever another country makes a diplomatic overture that requires a response from you. You may receive offers of peace when you are at war, offers of alliances and pacts from other great powers, and offers from minor nations to intervene in a war on their behalf. In all cases your choice is to accept or reject the diplomatic offer.

The results of diplomatic offers are reported in the turn summary at the beginning of each turn.
3162:
Information presented on the offer sheet beneath the map informs you of the type of offer your country received.

While looking at the offer, a world map provides geographic information about the countries involved. For more information click on the yellow "i" icon at the top of the screen.  Now you may select different countries by clicking on the map and also cycle between the four informational settings using  the small icons in the middle of the upper panel.  

This information might help you decide whether to accept or reject the offer based on the alliances in the world, on the strength of various diplomatic relationships, or on which nations are at war and which are at peace.  A warning is supplied on the offer itself if acceptance has serious consequences not immediately apparent. 

Much of the available information is similar to what you obtain when conducting diplomacy during your turn. However, during the diplomatic offers phase you are able to see small icons on the map representing all the current diplomatic offers of all the Great Powers.
3163:
You will receive alliance offers when other Great Powers perceive you to be very strong, or when they are desperate for help. It’s almost always a good idea to accept alliance offers, especially early in the game. 

The only time you should decline is if you will be dragged into a war that is ongoing between your new ally and their enemies. Such consequences, if any, will be listed beneath the offer.
3164:
Alliances are only made between Great Powers. Pacts, while they can be accepted  by minor nations, will never be offered by them. A Minor Nation is always glad to receive a pact from Great Power.

When you offer a non-aggression pact you are making a promise not to declare war on that nation. This means that as long as you keep your word, you will be unable to attack that nation in any way. Of course, you can break the pact and declare war but the diplomatic cost of war (mainly penalties involving world opinion) are much more severe when you break a pact.

Agreeing to an Alliance is more serious. You are making a promise to declare war on any great power that declares war on your ally. The ally is making the same promise to you. Should you refuse to declare war and uphold the alliance, severe diplomatic penalties apply. However, if the ally is the aggressor, not the defender, you may decide not to support the ally and suffer no penalty.
3165:
When an Old World  Neutral State has been attacked by a Great Power its leaders often seek a friendly Great Power to declare war on their enemy and protect their nation. This action by a Great Power is called intervention.

You receive offers to intervene only if you are the Great Power with the best relationship to the attacked Minor Nation and only from a Minor Nation in which you have an embassy.

If you accept the offer to intervene, you pay all normal penalties for declaring war on the Great Power. However, the benefits of intervention are significant. You immediately acquire the Minor Nation as a colony. You gain control over all their armed forces and can deploy more regiments to defend their provinces. 

You will not receive offers to intervene from tribes in the New World, even if your country is very friendly with them because Great Powers simply attack tribes, they do not declare war first. The only way to protect a tribe from other Great powers is to use a merchant unit and purchase land in all of the provinces of the tribe.  In order for another Great Power to attack a New World province in which your country owns land, the aggressor must first declare war on you. It is never necessary to declare war on a tribe.
3171:
This screen reports all battles on land or sea that occur in the world each turn. Whether you resolve battles on the tactical battlefield, or with strategic combat resolution, the results are reported here. Extra details are supplied if your forces were involved in the battle. otherwise you receive only a summary.

You can review these results again during your next turn by clicking on the information  button in the upper right corner of the toolbar, and then clicking on the battle report button on the information dialog.
3172:
The red banner at the top of the screen tells you which Great Power was victorious and displays a list of the forces engaged in the battle. The location of the battle is displayed by an icon on the map.

You may cycle either using the two arrow buttons, or by selecting a different battle icon on the map. The icon for the selected battle flashes. The icon is color-coded according to the results of the battle. Red means your forces were defeated. Green means you won a victory. White means the battle did not involve your fleets or armies.
3173:
Whenever your own Empire’s forces are engaged the large "I" button (top center of the screen) is active and will be colored gold. Click on this "i" to bring a detailed unit by unit list of the forces involved in the battle. 

On the screen that appears you see the wounds suffered by the two forces, and may also receive notice of special losses or gains as a result of this fight. For instance your fleet may intercept resources from enemy shipping, or your armies may plunder the provinces of your foes.

This screen does not require any orders from you; it is informational only. Once the new turn begins you may wish to alter the missions of your fleets or move wounded armies out of dangerous areas, based on the results you see here.
3174:
You can protect Tribes by buying their land using the Merchant. Once you own land in a province, no other Great Power can attack that province without first declaring war on you.  Since Tribes themselves are not protected by the rules of diplomacy that apply in the Old World, this is one good way to slow down the other Great Powers’ conquest of the New World. 

It is important to buy land in tribal capitals before you buy in their other provinces. Otherwise, another Great Power could conquer the capital. Anarchy would ensue,  you would lose your investments in the outlying tribal provinces and they would no longer benefit from your protection.
3181:
When the battle begins, you will see a dialog with a small map showing you where in the world this battle is taking place. On this dialog you can choose to deploy units yourself or delegate the job to the computer. If you deploy your own forces, green dots displayed on the battlefield show where you can place them.

Click on a green dot to deploy a regiment to that location.

The deployment area is always outside the range of the enemy units.
3182:
Once both sides have deployed their forces,  The attacker receives the first turn. Just as on the terrain map, there is a unit cycle that selects each unit in turn. You may choose to move your units in any order desired however. 

To select a unit out of the order presented, hold your mouse over the unit and click when you see the small blue flag and arrow cursor. 

On the map surrounding the selected unit you will see small dots (either red or green) Place your mouse over a dot and click when you see the soldier cursor. The selected unit immediately moves to the new location. Green dots mark areas that are currently safe, although the enemy may be able to attack those spaces on his turn.

If your unit is in range of an enemy with firearms or cannon, a crosshairs cursor appears over the enemy unit. If your unit has already fired, you see a unloaded gun. When you are next to an enemy a crossed swords (melee) cursor appears over the enemy unit. Clicking on an enemy unit attacks it.
3183:
The Bottom bar displays the information about the selected regiment in the green box surrounded by a gold line. As you place your cursor over other items on the bottom bar or on the map, the gray box will supply additional information. Placing your cursor over enemy units can give you a better idea about which enemies to attack first.

The "next unit" button is silver with a soldier and small gold arrow pointing to the right. Click on this button during your turn to cycle through all friendly units.

The "done with unit "button is silver with a soldier and an exclamation point. If you choose to reserve your fire or to move only part of your movement points, you can to click here to advance the game to the next unit. Once a unit is done it may not be selected again this turn.

The green button with a gold arrow is used to retreat all your units at once.  You should click here only if the battle is lost and retreating might save the lives of some valuable regiments.

At the far right side of the bottom bar is a green button with an exclamation point. This ends your turn and allows the enemy to begin its turn.

Fighting on a tactical battlefield gives you the best chance for a crushing victory over your enemies. This option may be turned off using the preferences screen at any time during your turn. Once you enter the tactical battlefield, you are committed to fighting there, but you may choose to let your computer advisor handle the battle for you.
3184:
Once both sides have deployed their forces the battle is fought in turns .  The attacker moves and fights with all of his forces, and then the defender does the same.

One of the most important concepts on the tactical battlefield is opportunity fire. If a unit does not fire on its turn then it has reserved its fire for any opportunity that may occur during the other player's turn. You can tell at a glance whether any units on the battlefield currently have reserved their fire by looking at the small colored box near each unit. If that box has a white outline, it means the unit does have fire reserved for opportunities.

If no units with any attacking potential present themselves as targets, the opportunity fire is directed at other units. This happens once the other player has ended his move, prior to the start of the new turn.

Additionally, melee and firing are  two different forms of combat. This means that in melee combat, the defender strikes back even on the attacker's turn.  Any attack on an adjacent unit is a melee attack.  Some units are much better at one form of combat. For instance pikemen can fight only in melee. All artillery units are exceptionally weak in melee.
3185: The best way to conduct an attack is concentration of force against a small number of defenders. Use light cavalry and light infantry to draw fire from stationary defenders, and then move in your heavy forces (Heavy Infantry and Heavy Cavalry are best) and destroy the line of enemies one by one. Use your artillery to weaken the better enemy defenders before your best regiments close with them. The most important rule is to concentrate your strength against one enemy (as far as possible) until that unit is out of action.
3186:
Early forts are usually level 1 (wood) and include one regiment of emplaced artillery. Unless these forts are reinforced by mobile regiments they can always be taken by three units of the proper type.

The ideal force for an assault on a non-reinforced fort consists of light artillery and some light infantry (not peasants) or other unit with a firearm such as an arquebusier or a musketeer. The minimum amount for success is two horse artillery and one other unit. This force can take a wooden fort with the earliest form of emplaced gun.  The method is to advance the non-artillery regiment leaving the artillery out of range. The infantry regiment draws the opportunity fire of the emplaced gun, and then takes the second attack of the enemy on the enemy’s turn. Then, when the light artillery advances, there is no opportunity for the emplaced gun to fire at it.  

Because emplaced artillery cannot move, an attacker who brings the proper force to take an unoccupied fort can always win. The defender has no options except to fire his emplaced guns and wait to be destroyed. Even though forts might seem very strong when you first start to play, eventually forts need extra mobile units in them to be safe, especially extra heavy artillery.

For advice on taking strongly defended forts, consult your Imperialism II manual.
3187:
The display for each regiment on the battlefield includes a damage bar. The amount of green on this bar tells you roughly how many of the regiment's troops are able to fire.  A damaged regiment's firepower is modified by a multiplier equal to the percentage of forces that are effective. A damaged unit is not only closer to retreating, it is also weaker when it attacks.

As the regiment is fired upon, the bar turns partly yellow and/or red. When there is no green anywhere on the bar the unit is considered broken. It will surrender if surrounded and will otherwise flee from the battle as rapidly as possible. 

The length of the red area on the bar tells you what proportion of the force of this regiment are permanently (for this battle) out of action. These troops are killed, wounded or fled off the battlefield.  If a bar turns entirely red (with no yellow) the regiment is destroyed and cannot ever be reformed.

The length of the yellow area tells you the proportion of troops that are still capable, but are no longer fighting due to poor morale. These troops can be rallied by a general.

Most regiments flee from battle before they are destroyed. Generals are used to prevent this from occurring. When a general is the active unit, move him adjacent to any of your regiments who have suffered damage, and click on the general unit. Morale will be restored to all units adjacent to the General according to the ability of the General. 

Overuse of a General can cause a weakened regiment to be killed outright, as it remains on the battlefield. You should consider letting a broken unit retreat if it is near death.
3188:
The small button with a star on it orders the selected unit to move under computer control. If you want to fight the entire battle this way, click on the lock button next to it.  You can regain control by clicking on the lock again.

Be cautious using this feature especially when the two forces are of relatively equal strength. You might find that your computer advisor is not as careful with your regiments as you would be.
3211:
At the end of every trade offers phase, before the new turn begins, the Deal Book is displayed.  If you want to look at the Deal Book again during your turn, it may be brought up through the Information dialog. 

The information dialog is opened when you click on the "i" button in the upper right corner of the toolbar,
3212:
The Deal Book lists all your country's trades, as well as potential deals that did not happen because you rejected them or ran out of cargo holds. If a deal improved the diplomatic relations between the two countries it will be noted in the deal book.

From the deal book, you can access the markets scroll by clicking on one of the commodity icons on the right side of the screen. The information displayed here is for the turn that just ended. 

The deal book also provides an end of turn summary, called the bottom line, that reports your profits or losses for the turn.
3213:
At the beginning of the game your country’s trade balance depends on the value of what you sell minus the expense of what you buy. Often it can be a good idea to buy more than you sell to help your economy get off to a fast start. Eventually, as your cash is depleted, you need to make money.  The most obvious method is to sell more of your materials, but there are two alternatives.

Your Empire can receive overseas profits only by using a merchant unit and buying land in a Neutral State or Tribe. Once the merchant buys the land it can be developed by builders and connected by engineers. The commodities will be offered for sale by the other country each turn. Often, you may choose to buy these resources yourself.  Of course you have to pay for them, but after this cost is deducted, the other country returns to you a percentage of the sale price based on the strength of the diplomatic relationship between the two countries.  You make more money when some other country buys the products your units developed. In this case the Neutral state passes part of the profits collected from the buyer directly to your coffers. All the profits returned to your Empire from foreign lands you develop are reported on the deal book balance sheet as overseas profits.

Liquidated riches refers to spices, silver, gold, gems and diamonds--either purchased from a tribe, or transported from New World land you conquer. These riches do not need to be resold or produced into anything else. As soon as they reach your capital city they convert immediately to cash. The amount is reported on the deal book balance sheet each turn.
3214:
Sometimes you may spend too much money and end a trade offers phase in the red. The Deal Book informs you of this fact and lists your borrowing limit. If you go over this limit you will receive a warning about a forced sale of your warehouse stockpile. The prices paid during a forced sale are quite low and it is a good idea to avoid it if you can. Additionally, you cannot purchase anything during your turn, nor can you give orders that require an expenditure, as long as you are too far in debt.

On the other hand, there is nothing wrong with borrowing as long as you stay within your credit limit. In fact, since the world banking community likes to have your country in debt, every time you borrow and then repay the money your credit limit for the future increases. Credit limit also depends on the technology successfully researched by your Great Power.
3221:
When a land garrison is selected, the encampment of the garrison shows a flashing white outline. The units in this garrison appear in the toolbar display. The first step, using the toolbar, is to select the regiments you want. You are selecting units for movement orders; it is not necessary to give regiments orders to stay behind and defend. Units remaining at the end of the turn will automatically defend the province from attack.

The toolbar arrows do not permit you to select particular regiments of a single category. If you want to make a more specific selection of forces you can use the Garrison Book. This is necessary, for instance, if you want a particular veteran regiment of Heavy Cavalry, among several present in the garrison, to conduct an attack.
3222:
There are two ways you can move your selected army on the map in your own provinces. The cursor shows the type of movement a click on a given province would order. 

If you want to move to an adjacent friendly province, click on that province with the marching soldier cursor. 

If you want to move the selected army further, but still in friendly territory, click with the train cursor which appears over the distant friendly province.
3223:
To enter an Old World province you do not own, you must first declare war on the owner of the province. On subsequent turns, any adjacent units may attack.

You do not have to declare war on a Tribe. You may attack without warning.

Unless you conduct a landing mission with a fleet,  you cannot attack unless your forces are adjacent to the target province. The attack is made by clicking on the target province with the crossed swords cursor.

When you have ordered the attack a large red military arrow appears in the enemy province. To cancel the attack click on the military arrow with the question mark cursor.
3224:
Once your fleets establish a landing site, you select land forces and use the crossed sword attack cursor to order them to move directly across the seas to the enemy province. 

On the first turn:
• Make sure you have a selected fleet in a sea zone adjacent to the province you want to invade.
• Place your mouse cursor over the coastline of the enemy province. Click when you see a cannon cursor. The fleet moves to a point near the coast and is shown with a cannon icon that lets you know it is conducting a landing.
• Make sure you have land forces somewhere in your Empire in a province that has a port. Next turn, only troops in ports will be able to invade. Your capital city is a port.

On the second turn:
• Select the land forces that you want to use to invade the enemy province. Their pictures should be in the toolbar. Use the arrows in the toolbar to select a force of the right size. Fleets can land one regiment for every cargo hold they possess.
• With the troops selected, click on the enemy province with a crossed swords cursor. A red attack arrow appears over the province that represents your invading forces.
3225:
The first military command button, which appears as a flag, brings up a detailed book on the selected garrison.  You may also view this book by clicking with the blue question mark cursor directly on the garrison encampment.

The garrison book shows the state of the selected garrison, including the names, the health, and the medals of each regiment. By clicking on the picture of a unit you may select or unselect it individually.  As you select a unit in the book  the toolbar numbers of selected units change to reflect your selection.

That same button also works when a fleet is selected, showing details about the selected fleet.
3231:
When a fleet is selected the ship icon shows a flashing white outline. The ships in this fleet appear in the toolbar display. The first step, using the arrows in the toolbar, is to select the ships you want to command. You select ships for movement or mission orders. 

Normally, all the ships are selected by default.  If you want only a portion of your ships to perform a mission or move, you can control which ships are selected with the arrows in the toolbar next to each ship type. 

When you give movement orders, the ships not contained in your selection remain behind. The toolbar arrows do not permit you to select particular ships of a single category. If you want to make a more specific selection of forces you can use the fleet book.
3232:
Once you have made a selection of ships using the toolbar or the fleet book, use a map cursor to command it. The map cursors allow you to assign your selected fleet in four different ways: movement to another sea zone plus three kinds of missions. 

To move the fleet, click on a new sea zone with the ship's wheel cursor.  This cursor does not appear in the fleet's current sea zone. If the new zone is out of range you see a red slashed circle cursor;  you cannot move the fleet that far in one turn.
3233:
In its current sea zone a fleet can patrol, attempting to intercept all hostile ships, by using the telescope cursor. A fleet can blockade a designated port, using a ship with a red X cursor, by clicking near the port when that cursor appears. Both of these commands are used against enemy forces. A blockade has greater chance of success against ships that enter or leave the selected port. A blockade does not seek other ships in the sea zone, but hostile patrolling fleets can intercept your blockaders. 

Both blockades and patrols can result in battle against hostile warships or in interception of merchant ships. When merchants are intercepted the intercepting forces can sink or capture the merchant ships. Additionally, it is possible to capture the cargo being carried. These details are summarized in the battle report at the end of the turn.
3234:
Near the coast you see a cannon cursor. This allows the fleet to establish a site for a later landing of army forces. When you assign fleets to this mission, you are accepting the potential of automatic interceptions by enemies. Any enemy fleet that enters the sea zone or patrols in the sea zone can find and intercept your forces. You must be prepared to defeat these attacks. 

You cannot move land forces on the turn the landing site is established. Land forces can be moved to the selected enemy province on any subsequent turns as long as you maintain the landing site by keeping ships in that sea zone.
3241:
You can use your diplomatic and trading skills and your civilian workers to help your Empire gain control of Minor nations and Tribes without the need for an invasion of their provinces.

Work performed by your civilian units in Minor Nations increases the production of resources by those nations once the developed resources are connected to a capital city or other port.  These resources are offered for purchase during each turn’s trading. 

Trade deals with Minor nations and tribes can improve your Empire’s relationship to the other nations and can eventually result in peaceful takeover.
3242:
Checklist for peaceful development:
• Send an Explorer abroad to look for valuable resources in other lands.
• Once you learn the diplomatic expertise technology,  establish an Embassy with at least one Minor Nation or Tribe.
• Once you learn the merchant companies technology, build a Merchant.
• Send the Merchant to the Minor Nation or Tribe to purchase land with valuable resources including riches. 
• To protect the tribe from extinction by other powers purchase land in the capital city province first.
• Once land is purchased, deploy a Builder to the land to increase its production and connect the land to a port using the Engineer.
• Bid on the Trade screen for the resources you've developed, or merely gain money when other Great Powers buy those products.
• If you have developed riches no trade bid will be required. Your ships will be assigned to move the riches to your homeland during the trade phase.
• View the success of your overseas developments in the Deal Book every turn.
3243:
Your Merchant is able to purchase land which contains horses, wool, cotton,  sugar, furs, tobacco, timber, iron, tin, copper, silver, spices, gold, diamonds, or gems, and eventually coal.  He cannot purchase land which produces only food. He can purchase land in minor nations or tribes where you have built an embassy.

To purchase a parcel of land with your selected Merchant look for the gold coins cursor, and click on the land you want. Once you see the asking price for the land you can confirm the purchase or change your mind.

Once a Merchant purchases land in a Tribe's province, that province is protected from Great Power invasion unless the invader is willing to declare war on the Great Power who bought the land. Since Tribes themselves are never protected by the rules of diplomacy that apply in the Old World, this is one good way to slow down the other Great Powers' conquest of the New World.
3244:
Once you purchase land with a Merchant, your  Builders and Engineers can build improvements and connect the tiles your bought to a port. These units work on terrain in Minor Nations just as they do in your own territory. Only connected tiles produce resources for trade.

As you gain new technology, you can send your civilians back to land you own in Minor Nations to further increase the resource output of the land.
3245:
Overseas profits are reported each turn on the Deal Book. You earn these profits for any resources produced on land you own in a Minor Nation that are sold by that Minor Nation during trade. 

If your Great Power purchases the resources itself, the overseas profits are a refund of the money you paid for them. This refund can reach 100% if you obtain a Minor Nation as a colony.

If another Great Power buys the resources, the money you earn comes from the pockets of your foe.
3251: You may choose to order your industry to produce materials each turn with any labor left over after you assign your production orders.  With this preference turned on, your labor is never wasted, but you might produce materials out of resources that you intended to save in the warehouse.
3252:
You can choose to resolve land battles on a strategic level or using tactical battlefields. For the tactical option set the tactical battle control on the preferences screen to Manual.  For the strategic option set this control to Automatic. Once you are on the battlefield using the manual option, you can still choose to resolve the tactical fights yourself or order your advisor to do so. Even if you give control to your advisor for part of the battle, you can take it back if necessary. Regardless of the mode of resolution, the same rules apply to all battles and a battle report will be shown to you to check results after the fight.

A human who is experienced with the tactical option may find that the computer does not fight as well as the human expects when the battles are resolved strategically.  Generally it is a good idea to attack with slightly larger forces when using strategic combat resolution.
3253:
The feedback window which is present during the tutorial can be set to appear during the regular game. The top part of the window shows feedback about the action you just took. The lower part prompts a possible next action.

It is usually best to leave warnings active. Warnings refer to notifications of specific events in the game or specific things you might want to alter. Even if you turn warnings off, "dire" warnings will still appear. Dire warnings usually refer to events that could cost you the game in the near future--such as the loss of your capital city.
3254: Sound or music may be turned off by moving the volume control all the way to the left side of the slider.
3255:
Animations shown in tactical battle include firing and attacking by regiments and death effects. Playing the animations slows the battles down marginally, and does not supply any additional information.

Civilian unit animations play when a unit is working. When these are turned off it can be difficult to tell if a given unit is working on a project or available for a new assignment.
3256:
The turn summary and the deal book both supply useful information and normally appear automatically prior to each new turn. You can speed up the game by not showing them, but you risk missing important information especially in the turn summary.

Both the turn summary and the deal book can be accessed during your turn using the information dialog. Click on the "i" button at the top of the toolbar, and on the dialog that comes up click on "deal book" or "turn summary".
3261: Greetings, Your Majesty. As the ruler of a burgeoning Empire you enjoy a vast amount of power over political, military, and economic affairs. These Briefings will be presented to help you learn the interfaces through which you issue your commands.
3262:
You may reopen a Briefing, or reach the Imperialism help menu through the help and information button in the upper right corner of most screens. 

You can take advantage of hot text messages on most screens by placing the cursor over objects or pictures.   

When you want to know more about something, right mouse click on it.  Often, more information is available.
3263:
The world of Imperialism consists of provinces ruled by governors.  To win you must obtain the support of a majority of governors. 

The world-wide Council of Governors nominates two Great Powers for possible victory every 10 years.  To be nominated your country must expand its industry and economic clout. Once there are two nominees all the governors in the world vote for one of the two, or abstain from voting.

Owning, conquering or colonizing a province provides automatic support if your country is nominated to win.  

If your country is nominated, governors in other countries may choose to support you due to your diplomatic or military successes. Generally, provinces owned by Great Powers consider military threat when deciding to vote.  Minor Nation owned provinces, on the other hand, are more interested in the diplomatic prestige of the nominated Great Powers.

You might choose to play aggressively in one area of the world, and peacefully in another. A combination of military and diplomatic strategies will generally garner support the most quickly.
3264: The computer icon at the top of the toolbar on the map screen takes you to the game control menu. You should save your game every six turns or so. This menu also lets you enter the preferences screen. Here you set controls for animations, sound, music, tactical battles, and other options.
3265: As you give orders to your industry, traders, diplomats, civilian workers, and military, the rulers of other empires do the same. Your orders can be canceled at any time prior to clicking the End Turn button at the bottom of the toolbar on the map screen. When you click this button and the turn ends, the orders of all Great Powers are carried out simultaneously.
3281:
Scroll around your country to find a good place for your capital city.  The framed area around a potential site tells you what sort of terrain will be immediately available for use if you found your city there.

If you are curious about a potential city site, click on the tile. A pop-up window will inform you of the resources immediately available at that site. 

You can still cancel your selection after considering this resource report.
3282: Food resources are the most important early in the game. The best city sites are adjacent to a mixture of grain from farms,  and meat from seas, rivers and open range . Your workers, your military regiments,  and your ships each eat one unit of food (either grain or meat) every turn.
3283:
Timber and wool are two of the most important industrial resources early in the game, so you should look for a site adjacent to scrub or hardwood forest, or adjacent to fertile hills. Iron ore is equally important; but, since it must be prospected for, you cannot know for sure where it is.

A good city site tends to be near those resources that are not immediately adjacent so you can access them rapidly once the game begins. For instance a site within five tiles of a large number of hills and mountains is likely to be close to iron ore. A site that is not adjacent to any wool or timber should at least be near them for rapid development.
3284: If you cannot find a city site near valuable resources and with sufficient food, you should consider returning to the Map Room to generate a different random world.
3285:
Click on the large button with the curved arrow at the top of the toolbar to return to the Map Room. On this screen you have the choice of selecting a different country in this same world, or generating an entirely new world.

The first world generated as the globe spins will be the same one. Click on a different colored Great Power, and then on Start Game.

Click on the globe again to create a new world.
3291:
The status screens provide comparisons between all the Great Powers in a variety of fields. The ratings on each screen go from top to bottom and the length of the colored bar shows how competitive the various Powers are in each category. 

The first tab provides an assessment of the power of the various Great Powers in the game.  The country that is ahead in this category may not actually be winning the game in terms of number of provinces controlled in the Old World.  However, the leading countries in this rating are in some sense the most dangerous. Often these countries have the capability to expand their Empires rapidly when necessary.
3292:
The four lower tabs on the left side of the screen compare the status of the Great Powers in terms of interior strength, diplomatic strength, land military strength, and naval strength.

Interior strength compares the maximum amount of resources and materials each Empire could transport within its borders. This gives you a good idea of the infrastructure developed by each power and the resources available to it for rapid future expansion.

To compare the diplomatic strength of the Great Powers, the relations of each power with all the other countries in the world is averaged. Often the leading powers in this category are at peace, and may be planning to obtain control of other nations through diplomacy and economics.

The comparison of the land military strength measures both number and quality of the regiments. Great Powers often choose to attack powers that appear weak in this comparison. Try to keep your nation out of last place.

The naval comparison is also used by other nations to decide which powers to attack.
3293:
The tabs labeled world exports and overseas profits on the right side of the status screen can give you a good idea of the trading and overseas strength of the various empires, as well as their income levels.

World exports measures the value of all commodities sold to other nations over the past several turns. It is weighted to count more recent turns as more valuable than past turns to give you an better idea of which countries are strongest right now.

Overseas profits refer to money earned by the sale of resources and materials developed in other nations.  Some Great Powers will choose to conquer new lands before developing them,  and these countries will not show any overseas profits.
3294:
The statistics of industry, labor, and technology  give you  a good idea of the strength of the Great Powers’ economies. 

Industry measures the amount of materials produced by each Great Power over the past several turns, weighted to make more recent turns more important.

Labor is the current total of available labor of each great Power.

Technology  measures the number and era of the technologies each country has discovered. You can get details on which power has learned which technology using the small flags on the technology screen itself.
3301: You may reach the diplomacy screen from the main map by clicking on the scroll icon on the gold ribbon at the bottom of the screen.
3302:
When you first bring up the diplomacy screen notice that the colored oval "i" button in the upper left is selected. This means that you are looking at the information panel of the diplomacy screen.

In the middle of the upper part of the screen you see four small vertical icons which allow you to see four different types of information while you are on this panel. As you click on these icons the map changes to display the type of information represented by each small icon.

By clicking on any country on the map you see the information about that particular country.
3303:
The information panel can help you choose a minor nation to pursue. You could randomly select a country to try to trade with, but it is more efficient to consider what commodities it is trading.

First, make sure that you are on the information panel by clicking on the colored "i" oval. The letter i should be surrounded with white.

Next, click on the lowest of the four vertical icons. This looks like a small coin.

Finally, cycle through the six old world minor nations on the map (by clicking on each in turn). These nations are all colored different shades of gray. As you select each one, a list of the products it exports will appear above the map. Remember the name of the nation that seems best to you. You should consider selecting a nation with commodities currently in short supply.
3304:
Offering a trade consulate is a diplomatic overture that increases the benefits of trading. Once you have a consulate in a minor nation, all trades with that nation improve your diplomatic relationship, and you can set helpful trade policies. Eventually, after many years of friendly trading, this nation can join your Empire peacefully.

To offer a trade consulate click on the green oval with the scroll near the top of the screen. This takes you to the overtures panel. 

Click on the large scroll labeled Trade Consulate. This selects the type of overture.

Click on the country on the map you want to offer the consulate to. You see a coin appear over the nation on the map. Trade consulates are always accepted and cost $500.
3305:
You cannot use the diplomacy screen to encourage trade with a country the same turn you offer the consulate. Once you have a consulate a helpful trade policy can be set.

On the diplomacy screen, click on the turquoise trade policies oval at the top of the screen. This takes you to the trade policies panel. 

Select the percentage of trade subsidy you wish to grant. The larger the percentage, the more the other country will appreciate your Empire. Of course this reduces your profits and increases the cost of commodities you purchase.

Click on the country on the map. A gold circle with the percentage amount appears on the screen. Trade subsidies take effect immediately.

Power tip: hold the control key down while clicking on the country. The computer will automatically select the correct subsidy to make you the selected country’s most favored trade partner.
3311: You may reach the trade screen from the main map by clicking on the coins icon on the gold ribbon at the bottom of the screen.
3312:
To buy commodities in trade you must enter a bid. You can enter bids on three or fewer commodities (research can allow you to increase that number). Bids do not guarantee that you will be able to buy what you want. By bidding you are letting the rest of the world know that you desire that commodity.

To enter a bid click on the "B" in the commodity row corresponding to the commodity you want to buy.
3313:
To sell commodities in trade you must enter an offer. You can enter offers on as many of your commodities as you wish. Offers do not guarantee that you will be able to sell the commodities. By offering you are letting the rest of the world know that you want to sell that commodity.

To enter an offer click on the "O" in the commodity row corresponding to the commodity you want to sell. A slider appears allowing you to set the quantity offered this turn. The quantity offered for sale cannot exceed the amount of ship cargo holds you have assigned to trade. You can see what this number is on the right side of the trade screen.
3314:
When you end your turn the offers and bids of all countries in the game are compared. For commodities you bid on, you are presented with offer sheets listing the country offering the commodity, the price, and the maximum you can buy. 

To accept an offer, click the accept seal. To accept a lesser amount than is offered, change the number in the gray box and then click the accept seal. 

To stop seeing offers of a particular commodity, click in the No more offers of... box on the offer sheet. To reject any offer, click on the reject seal.

As you are responding to other countries' offers, those countries that bid on commodities you offered may be buying your items. You will not see an offer sheet for these deals, since it is always up to the bidder (not the offering nation) to finalize each deal.
3315:
As each deal is finalized some of the cargo holds you have assigned to trade may be used to transport the commodities. You can keep track of how many cargo holds you have remaining by looking at the number under the ship on the right side of the screen. When the last cargo hold is used, you will receive no more offer sheets this turn. Each cargo hold can be used only once per turn.

The basic rule for pickup and delivery is that the nation who buys the commodities (the bidder) picks up the commodities in its own ships. Therefore on all deals in which you accept an offer,  your Empire's cargo holds will be used up for the turn. 

If the buyer is not a Great Power, they have no ships. This means that offers you (and the other Great powers) made that were purchased by tribes or minor nations require Great Power cargo holds for delivery.
3316:
The deal summary may show that someone offered you a commodity, but you didn’t ever see the offer sheet. 

When an offer is about to be made to you, the computer checks to see if you have any ships left to pickup the goods. If you don’t, then you aren’t shown the offer because you wouldn’t be allowed to accept it. Sometimes you have fewer cargo holds than you expected because they were used to make deliveries of materials you sold to other nations. However, you are informed in the report that the country was willing to make the deal. That way you can plan to reserve ships next time if you want to.
3317:
There are three reasons why you may not be seeing any trade offers: 

1. You haven’t bid on anything. Go to the Trade Orders screen and make sure you have clicked on some buy bids.

2. You don’t have any ships available for picking up the goods. If that is the case, you need to free up some ships for trade. You could reduce your transport orders by ship. You could bring home an exploring ship and dock it in the capital harbor. You could build a new ship.

3. No one is offering to sell the item you bid on. If that is case, bid on something else. Wool and timber are usually being offered for sale. You can check if anyone offered an item you bid on from the deal summary screen. Click on the icon of that item on the right to bring up the market summary for that item. The nations who offered it are shown on the left.
3321: Like the production and labor screens, the unit construction screen is considered part of Industry.  From the main map you reach all three screens by clicking on the icon of a factory on the gold ribbon. Once you are within industry you can use all of the screens, alternating between them by using the three icons in the gold banner at the top of the screen. Labor is represented by a hammer, production is represented by a gear, and unit construction is represented by crossed flags.
3322:
First, select the unit that you want to build by clicking on its picture in one of the panels on the right side of the screen. The selected type of unit appears in the large box on the left side of the screen, and the text provides details about the unit.

In the middle of this build panel are icons and numbers which tell you the cost of the unit. When you lack the necessary amount of a commodity it is shown with a red x superimposed. Above the costs you see two gold arrows and a small text box.

Click the right arrow to increase the number you are building, and the left arrow to decrease. The number you have ordered appears in the text box and near the unit picture on the right side of the screen. All units take one turn to build and are available for action next turn.

All military and naval units require a peasant laborer. Like workers in industry, each military or naval unit eats food each turn. If you build too many units too quickly, your industry will not have enough labor to continue to develop.
3323:
First, select the unit that you want to build by clicking on its picture in one of the panels on the right side of the screen. The selected type of unit appears in the large box on the left side of the screen. All civilians cost 3 paper and $500. If you lack the required paper or money a red x will appear. 

Click the right arrow to increase the number you are building, and the left arrow to decrease. The number you have ordered appears in the text box and near the unit picture on the right side of the screen. All units take one turn to build and are available for action next turn. Unlike military and naval units civilian units do not require a peasant for construction, nor do they eat any food.

Note that it is not possible to delegate unit construction to the computer.
3331:
Building 3 new regiments of Pikemen requires 3 available Peasant workers. If you haven’t recruited more Peasants than was required in the Labor episode, you will need to do so now. 

Even if you have recruited enough Peasants, you may still face a shortage if they are busy working on production orders. You can tell at a glance how many Peasants you have and how many are working:  under the labor icon (hammer) in the left scroll, there are two numbers which show the available labor and the total labor.  Each Peasant unit represents 1 unit of labor. 

To free up working peasants, go the Production panel and decrease some production orders.
3341:
Early in the game it is often best to attack a relatively poorly defended province. Therefore, avoid the capitals, and avoid the provinces whose army size is shown as three tents. Pick a province whose army size is shown as two tents. Info-click on the map if you aren’t sure which is a capital and which isn’t.

It’s also a good idea to choose a province which contains some resources you would like to develop. 

Although wars in the Old World must be declared in advance, your Empire need not provide such a warning to a New World tribe.
3342:
Fleets can carry an invasion force whose size is equal to the number of cargo holds in the fleet. Each of your Carracks has three cargo holds. Therefore, one of your ships will be able to carry the three Pikemen you made in the last episode. 

Those three Pikemen are pretty tough, and have a good chance of success. However, they may be defeated and have to retreat back to your own land. If you decide to send a larger force, you will have to send more than one ship.

Remember not to move the last ship out of your home fleet. Although you can de-emphasize trade while conducting your invasion, at least one ship should remain behind for sea transport and/or a minimal amount of trade.
3343:
Once you know which ships are going to conduct the invasion order them to move (using the ship's wheel cursor) to any sea zone adjacent to the province you want to invade. This may take several turns.

If the ships for your invasion force are coming from different locations on the map--that's fine--have them meet in the same sea zone adjacent to the target province. They will combine into one fleet in the sea zone.
3344:
First, make sure that all ships are in the same sea zone and do not have any other missions. If some of the ships are patrolling or doing some other mission in the sea zone, cancel those orders first. (To cancel an unwanted mission click on the fleet icon when the question mark cursor is shown. A pop-up box appears informing you of the fleet's current mission. Click the Rescind button on the dialog box.)

You should select the invasion fleet and make sure all ships in the fleet are selected using the toolbar arrows. Remember that ships in a fleet are selected for a mission by increasing the number of ships shown in the gray box in the toolbar. Get those numbers as high as possible.

Then click on the adjacent province to be invaded; the cursor should look like a cannon. The fleet icon moves near the coast and a small cannon icon appears near the fleet. 

Establishing a  beachhead takes one turn, so you cannot send in the troops yet. End your turn and the episode will end. In the next episode you will send the troops in.
3345:
Your 3 Pikemen are waiting while the navy establishes a beachhead. When they come up in the cycle, just click the ‘No more Orders’ button, which tells the Pikemen you have no orders for this turn, but that you expect to see them come up in the unit cycle next turn.

Next turn when they come up, after you have established the beachhead, you will give them the attack order.
3351:
Military units are represented on the map by an encampment near the city or town in a province. Take a look at the area around your capital city. You see several small tents.

Move the cursor near the tents until you see a flag & arrow cursor. With this cursor showing click on the tents. The units that make up this garrison are displayed in the toolbar.

To select a force for movement or attacking, use the small arrows in the toolbar. The arrows pointing up increase the number of units selected for action and the arrows pointing down decrease this number.
3352:
To move (or deploy) units to a friendly province, make sure the proper units are selected and click on the province. A large green military arrow appears indicating that the force is on its way to that province. It will arrive next turn.

There is no need to deploy your units prior to attacking in this episode unless you have previously deployed some of them away from your capital. Your capital is the best place to launch the invasion because it is a port.
3353:
To attack into an adjacent province, select the forces and click on the enemy province to invade with a crossed swords cursor. A red attack arrow appears on the map, confirming your orders. It is not possible to attack non-adjacent enemy provinces unless you first establish a beachhead.

You do not need to attack adjacent provinces to complete this episode since you are conducting an overseas invasion.
3354:
In the last episode you used your fleet to establish a beachhead. You may select military units to invade up to the number of cargo holds in your invasion fleet.

With the proper sized force selected, scroll to the province on the map that contains your beachhead. A crossed swords cursor appears over the province. Click on the province. A red invasion arrow appears confirming your orders.
3355:
When you end your turn the battle will be fought. Results are provided on a battle report screen that lists the forces involved on both sides and reports any eliminated units.

You can view details of a battle by clicking the large gold ‘I’ button in the upper center of the battle report screen.

If you failed to take the province, build up and try again. Your invasion remains on station until you reassign it or the invasion succeeds.

Note that if you manage to take a tribal capital, rather than a village, you will receive valuable spoils of war.
3361: You may reach the technology screen from the main map by clicking on the compass icon in the gold ribbon at the bottom of the screen.
3362:
A new project is started by moving a listed "researchable" technology from the right side of the screen to one of the open available slots on the left side of the screen.

First,  to see a list of all your researchable technologies, make sure that the middle of the three gold medallions is highlighted in white. This medallion lists the technology currently available for research on the right side of the screen.  Also make sure that the "show all" filter button above the listed technologies is selected. 

Pick a technology to research from this list. Click on the compass button next to the text describing the technology. One of your available slots on the left side is filled with your selection.

Now you may allocate additional cash to the project using the slider in that slot. The more cash spent, the faster you will gain the benefits of the new technology.
3363:
Note: When a project is canceled all cash spent so far is lost. It is not applied to a newly selected project.

Click on the skull button in the slot of the unwanted project. The slot becomes available. You will be asked to confirm.
3364:
Turn control of research over to your computer advisor by clicking on the button in the gold ribbon on the top left part of the screen.

If you turn control of the technology screen over to the computer it will establish a long-term research goal for you and fill in all of your open slots. It will also allocate cash each turn.

One good way to play, especially for beginners is to allow the computer to pick the projects.  Once this is done,  you can take control back by clicking on the computer button. Now you have control of the cash to be spent on each project.
3365:
Click on the third of the three medallions next to the scroll (nearest the bottom of the screen). 
This lists all projects available as long-term goals. From this list, choose a goal and click on its target icon. The technology will appear in the goal slot at the top left part of the screen.

Next, click on the middle medallion. Technologies that lead to your goal are listed at the top highlighted with green text. You can now fill as many slots as desired with technologies that lead to your goal. Of course, sometimes only one technology is available that will lead to the goal you picked.

Use the arrows in each research slot  to allocate per turn spending to each of the selected projects.
3366:
When other Great Powers already have a technology, a little flag with their country color appears in the description of that technology.  You have an increased chance of learning a new technology that another country already knows about. In fact, when other countries have previously researched a technology successfully, you may put that technology in a research slot, put no money in, and still eventually learn the new technology.

Your chances of stealing the knowledge of other nations in this way vastly increases if you have a spy in a country who has a technology you are researching. If you do place a spy, the flags will be marked with a tiny "s".
3371:
You can tell when a unit is working because it animates. 

When the unit is finished working, the animation ends and the unit stands still. 

When a unit is selected, it appears with a flashing white outline. 

If a unit appears grayed out, then it is not working, it is deploying to that tile (See ‘What does "deploying" mean?’).
3372:
"Deploying" means a unit is moving to a new tile, but isn’t doing any work immediately in that tile.

You may choose to deploy a unit to move it out of the way of another unit. 

In the context of army units, "deploying" means to move to another one of your provinces.
3373:
Yes, you can change your orders. 

Click on a busy (working or deploying) civilian unit (the question mark cursor will appear). A dialog pops up that tells you what the unit is doing and gives you an opportunity to confirm or rescind your orders. 

In general, throughout Imperialism II, you can always change your orders until you have ended your turn. This will be true not just for unit orders, but for trade, diplomacy, industrial, transport, technology and other orders.
3374:
Your country is made up of terrain tiles, which have the potential to produce different types of resources. Grain farms appear as yellow-gold planted fields. 

If you are not sure what type of terrain you are looking at, place the mouse cursor over the tile and look at the text in the upper right portion of the screen. You can also info-click on the tile (right-click or shift-click) for more detailed information.
3375:
Builders construct improvements on most types of terrain in the game. Each improvement built makes the tile more productive. 

First, confirm that the builder is selected. On the map he flashes with a white outline, and his picture appears in the toolbar on the right side of the screen. 

To order the builder to improve a grain farm move the mouse over a farm and look for a hammer cursor. Click on the tile. The builder moves into that tile and begins working on the farm. This is confirmed by a working animation. 

The Builder takes two turns to build a new farm or to improve an existing  farm.
3381:
To buy land from a Tribe, you must first buy an embassy. But you cannot buy an Embassy until you purchase a trade consulate. These two purchases cannot  be made on the same turn.  To buy a trade consulate or an embassy click on the appropriate large scroll and then on the Tribe on the diplomacy map.

If the Tribe you have chosen is not on the map it means you have not discovered the tribal capital. To conduct any form of diplomacy you must uncover the tile containing the capital of the Tribe. You can do this using ships and explorers units in the New World.
3382:
Look around with your Explorer before choosing to buy land from a tribe.  As you discover tribal capitals consider whether this would be a good place to buy land. Here are some factors:

1. It is better to buy land from a Tribe you have not already attacked. Tribes you have attacked dislike your Empire so you will not benefit as much from overseas profits. The amount of overseas profits on a commodity sale is  divided between the Tribe (or Neutral State) and the Great Power that bought the land. As the relationship improves, the Great Power receives a higher percentage on each sale.

2.  If you see small colored flags on tiles around the tribal capital it means that another Great Power already owns that land. You do not want to waste the money for an embassy only to learn that the land is no longer available.

3.  Finally, consider what resources you need. Buy land that produces resources your Empire lacks.  You can tell what sort of resource is produced in a tile by holding your mouse over the tile and reading the text at the top of the screen.  If you info-click on a tile you can obtain more detailed information. Remember that for this episode you are concerned only with tiles adjacent to a tribal capital containing a development.
3383:
Build a merchant like any other civilian unit. Go to the Unit Construction panel of the Industry screen.  You do this by clicking on the factory icon on the gold ribbon at the bottom of the screen. Then, on the Industry screen, click on the flags icon at the top of the screen.

On the unit construction panel you select the merchant unit. Then order one to be built using the small gold build arrows. You need 3 units of paper and $500 to buy a Merchant.

The merchant will be completed the turn after you order construction.
3384:
Look at the tiles adjacent to the tribal capital.   Choose a tile that produces resources you are interested in buying.  Often these will be resources in short supply in your Empire.

Make sure your Merchant unit is selected and appears in the toolbar. Place your mouse cursor over the tile you picked. The cursor changes to represent some coins. Click on the tile.

The merchant moves to the tile and a dialog appears asking you if you want to pay the prices requested by the Tribe. This is a one time cost. To buy the land click "OK".
3385:
Tiles purchased in tribal lands or in Neutral States display purchase flags in the color of the purchasing Great Power. These flags denote ownership of the land and serve to warn other Great Powers that they can no longer buy the land.

There are diplomatic consequences once tiles are purchased in Neutral States or in tribal lands.  In the Old World, the flag can indicate a risk that the Great Power who owns the land might intervene if another Great Power declares war on the Neutral State.

In the New World the presence of a flag in a province has a more definite consequence.  If a Great Power buys land in the New World, the province where the land is bought is safe from other Great Powers attacks, until they are willing to declare war on the Great Power which bought the land. Of course, attacks can still be made against other tribal provinces. Only provinces with a flag are protected.

This explains why the tribal capitals are important to protect. When a capital is taken, the Tribe dissolves. All the purchased land in other provinces of that Tribe is lost since the Tribe that made the sale is no more.  For this reason, you should protect the province containing the capital first, then look around for  land to buy in other provinces.
3391:
The rules on what resources Minor Nations can trade are just like the rules which apply to Great Powers: the resource tiles must be developed, and connected to the capital. 

Just as for Great Powers, Minor Nations start with the tiles adjacent to their capitals already developed. The Minor Nation offers the resources in these tiles for sale. So if you own any of these tiles, and the resources are purchased on the world trade market, you will receive Overseas Profits without doing any more work. 

However, Minor Nations do not develop any more tiles on their own. You can and should buy undeveloped land that is further from the capital, but there is more work involved. You must send in a Builder to develop the resources, and an Engineer to connect the tile to the capital. You can build ports, and developed resources connected to the ports will also be offered for sale. Note that you must own land before the Builder can develop it, but you do not need to own land where the Engineer builds roads and ports.
3392:
Overseas profits are obtained whenever any country in the game buys resources from developed land you own in another country. These resources are offered for trade every turn automatically. Of course, you receive no profit at all if nobody wants to purchase these commodities.

This problem can be dealt with if you bid on the commodities yourself. This is why it’s a good idea to develop products you are actually interested in buying. When you buy commodities you have developed you may be surprised to see an offer sheet listing the full price of the commodity. That’s okay. The offer sheet does not include the overseas profits involved.

When you buy products your country developed, the overseas profits are returned to you after the deal is completed. For details on how to calculates the overseas profits you can expect, see the help topic "Calculating overseas profits".
3393:
When selecting a New World commodity to buy land for and then trade for,  there are four main agricultural products to consider.

Cotton is valuable as a substitute for wool. If your homeland is short on wool, cotton is a good resource to purchase since you can make valuable fabric out it. Fabric is used to recruit labor, to build ships and regiments, and to sell for a profit.

Sugar Cane is used to produce refined sugar, a luxury product essential to the productivity of your more highly trained workers.  Tobacco and furs also produce essential luxuries usually in demand later in the game than sugar. 

Of these three products sugar is often the best first choice. Sugar is more common than the others, and the technologies that let your Empire benefit from this luxury are easier to obtain than the tobacco and fur related technologies.
3394:
The amount you receive in overseas profits is calculated as a percentage of the purchase price paid by the buyer. If you have the best possible diplomatic relationship with the Tribe which produces the commodities you will receive back 100% of the price. In this case, if you buy the product, the entire amount you paid is returned to you--so you get the commodity for free.

If your relationship with a Tribe is very bad, you will receive very little profit on the sale of the commodities you developed.  You can improve your relationship, and the percentage of each sale you receive, by making more trade deals with the Tribe. Even the deals which only happen because you developed the land, and bid on the commodity from it, improve your relationship.

Generally, your country’s position on the relationship spectrum with the Tribe selected on the diplomacy screen is a good guide to the level of overseas profits you will receive. If your country is denoted about halfway up the spectrum, you will receive about 50% of the sale price.
3395:
When you discover undeveloped land in a Minor Nation containing resources you covet, it's a good idea to make a plan for exploiting it.

You can conquer the province or you could buy the land. Either way, you will need to develop the tile with a Builder, and connect the tile to a port with the Engineer. 

If the coveted resources are riches, you will make more money at first if you conquer the province than if you buy the land. (See related topic "Riches"). So why buy the land and exploit it peacefully? Well, military conquest is expensive. You need to make the troops and continue to feed them. You need to pay for the cost of mounting the attack. You need to make enough troops to defend your homeland as well as your conquests. 

You can take advantage of the most land by using a mix of military and mercantile strategies.
3396:
Riches are special commodities (from least to most valuable, they are spices, silver, gold, gems, diamonds) which convert to cash when transported to your homeland. They are found only in the New World. 

If you conquer a New World province containing riches, develop the riches and connect them to a port, then you can transport them using the transport screen.  The money they bring in is shown on the Deal Book as 'Liquidated Riches'.

If you buy land containing riches, develop the riches and connect them to a port, then the Tribe will offer to sell you the riches. The price you pay the Tribe is a lot less than the money you will get once you bring the riches home. The money the riches are converted to is shown on the Deal Book as 'Liquidated Riches'.

Unlike other resources you develop on purchased land, riches will only be offered to you, not to any other Great Power. As with other resources, the price you pay the Tribe will go down as your relationship with them improves.
3411:
Engineers build roads from the tile where they begin the turn into the adjacent tile that you click. 

First, confirm that the engineer is selected. On the map he flashes with a white outline, and his picture appears in the toolbar on the right side of the screen. To make sure that you are giving an order to build a road, look for a road cursor (a wavy brown line) over terrain tiles adjacent to the selected engineer.

With the road cursor showing over the tile where you want the road to go, click on the map. The engineer moves into that tile and begins working on the road, confirmed by a working animation. 

It may take several turns to build the road, depending on the terrain. Flat terrain takes only one turn.
3412: To complete this episode your newly built farm must be on or adjacent to an unbroken road that goes to the capital city of your nation. When this is achieved the farm is connected. This means that grain from the farm is automatically used each turn to feed your population.
3413:
Being connected means that the resources produced in a tile can be transported back to the capital city.

A tile is considered connected if it either has connected road in it, or if it is adjacent to connected road (there are six tiles adjacent to each other tile), or if it is adjacent to a port or capital. 

A road is considered connected if it continues back in an unbroken line to the capital city, or to another port (which your Engineer will learn to build in a later episode).

Look at the help text in the top right to see if a tile is connected. It shows the production amount and the connection level of the tile currently under the cursor. If the Max Transport is more than 0, the tile is connected.
3414:
After you give orders to the currently selected unit, the next available unit automatically becomes selected. This is called the unit cycle.

There are three buttons which affect the unit cycle.  These buttons each give orders to the currently selected unit. 

Click the button on the far right to put the unit to sleep. That means the unit will stay where it is, doing nothing (in the case of civilian units, for military and naval units, that button tells them to stay still and defend).  This unit will not appear automatically again in the unit cycle. If you want to give orders to a sleeping unit, you need to click on it, or you could type ‘W’ to wake all the sleeping units. 

The middle button tells the unit you have no orders for it this turn, but that you expect to see it appear in the cycle next turn.

Use the left button when you want to give orders to this unit, but you want to wait until you’ve had a chance to give orders to other units first (perhaps to get them out of the way). This button advances the unit cycle to the next unit, and puts the current unit at the back of the cycle.
3421:
Your country may contain deposits of four different minerals: iron ore, copper, tin, and coal. The type of mineral that could be present depends on the type of terrain in the tile. Tin is found only in swamps. The other three are found in hills or mountains.  

If you are not sure what type of terrain you are looking at, place the mouse cursor over the tile and look at the text in the upper right portion of the screen. You can also info-click on the tile (right-click or shift-click) for more detailed information. 

Later in the tutorial you will search other countries for additional types of minerals.
3422:
First, confirm that the explorer is selected. On the map he flashes with a white outline, and his picture appears in the toolbar on the right side of the screen.  When the explorer is selected terrain tiles you have unsuccessfully prospected are shown with a pick axe and red X icon.

To order the explorer to prospect (search for minerals) move the mouse over an unprospected hill, mountain, or swamp in your country and look for an eye cursor. Click on the tile. The explorer moves into that tile and begins prospecting, confirmed by a working animation. 

Prospecting takes one turn. If you find a mineral this episode will end and a mineral icon will be shown in the prospected tile.
3431: Each turn all the terrain tiles with improvements on them produce resources.  Your nation gains these resources only when they are connected to the capital city. A road connection is made when an unbroken road may be traced from a tile on or adjacent to the terrain tile all the way back to the capital city.
3432:
Usually, you will be able to tell if an improved terrain tile is connected by looking at the map. If you are not sure, place the mouse cursor over the tile and look at the text in the upper right portion of the screen. You can also info-click on the tile (right-click or shift-click) for more detailed information.  The dialog box that appears when you info-click allows you to compare production level  (how many units of resources the tile is producing) with transport level (how many units are being moved to the capital each turn). 

A tile that is unconnected has a transport level of 0. At the beginning of the game your roads can move only one unit of resources from each tile, so your transport level for a connected tile is 1.
3441: You may reach the production screen from the main map by clicking on the small factory icon in the gold ribbon at the bottom of the screen.
3442:
The blue banner at the top of the production screen is called the warehouse. It lists all the resources and commodities your nation has this turn. 

If you are not sure which resource or material an icon represents, place the mouse over the icon and read the text on the gold banner in the upper right portion of the screen.

When you end your turn, resources you have connected to your capital city on the map are moved into the warehouse for use on the next turn. Materials you make on this screen are added to the warehouse for next turn as well.
3443:
Each of the production sliders uses different resources, but all sliders need two units of resources for every material produced.

To use a slider to make a material, click on the gold arrow at the right end of the slider. The slider bar changes color confirming the production order. You may also click within the slider bar to increase or decrease production. The resources are deducted when the orders are given, but the new material is not ready until the next turn. 

To reduce an order for production click on the gold arrow to the left end of the slider. The resources are returned to the warehouse. You can change your mind about what to produce as often as you like. Production orders are not final until you end your turn.

You may choose to assign your production to the computer using the button at the top left of the screen. The sliders will be filled in automatically.  There is no guarantee that the computer will share all your short term goals (such as finishing this episode).
3444:
The amount of any material you can produce is limited by the amount of resources you have on hand and by the amount of industrial labor available to make the materials.

On the left side of the production screen you see an icon of a peasant laborer with a number underneath him. That number tells you how many peasant laborers your industry has. Each peasant represents one unit of labor every turn.

Above the peasant laborers is an icon representing the total available labor for this turn. As you give production orders using the sliders this number goes down. Since it takes two units of labor to make one material, if this number reaches 0 or 1 you will be unable to make any more materials this turn.
3451:
Like the production screen discussed in the last episode, the labor screen is considered part of Industry.  From the main map you reach both these screens by clicking on the factory icon on the gold ribbon at the bottom of the screen. Once you are within industry you can use both screens, alternating between them by using the two icons in the gold banner at the top of the screen. Labor is represented by a hammer, while production is represented by a gear.

Note that you cannot delegate the recruiting or training of labor to computer control.

In a later episode a third icon (and screen) will be added to this banner.
3452: On the labor screen peasants are recruited by spending the material fabric. Click on the arrow at the right end of the slider to recruit more peasants. Be cautious in the number of peasants you recruit.
